(p-٥) Sūrat Yūsuf (Surah Yusuf)

Meccan in its entirety.

Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: except for four verses within it.

The third: that these verses refer to the letters with which the surah opens, and that they are signs of the Arabic Book. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: "the Clear" means its guidance and its right direction, said by Qatadah.

﴿So that you may understand﴾. ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾, meaning We explain to you the best of explanation; and the qassas (narrator) is the one who tells the story in its true form.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿When Joseph said to his father, "O my father, I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon"﴾. On this there are two opinions.

The first: he saw his brothers and his parents prostrating to him, so he mentioned them in pairs. By "eleven stars" he meant his brothers, by "the sun" his father Ya'qub (Jacob), and by "the moon" his mother Rahil (Rachel). He saw them prostrating to him, and so he expressed it with what he mentioned. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The second: he saw the eleven stars, the sun, and the moon prostrating to him, and he interpreted the stars as his brothers, the sun as his father, and the moon as his mother. This is the view of most scholars.

Ibn Jurayj said: the sun is his mother and the moon is his father, because of the feminine form of "sun" and the masculine form of "moon."

al-Suddi narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, from Jabir, who said: "A man from the Jews called Bustana came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, tell me about the stars that Joseph saw prostrating to him. What are their names?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained silent and did not answer with anything, so Jibril (Gabriel) descended to him with their names."

He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for him and said: "Will you believe if I tell you their names?" He said: "Yes."

So he said: "Jaryan, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Dhu al-Kiftayn, Qabis, al-Wathab, al-'Amudan, al-Faliq, al-Musbih, al-Daruh, Dhu al-Far', al-Diya' and al-Nur." The Jew said: "By Allah, yes, these are indeed their names."

As for the repetition of his words, ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾, there are two explanations. The first: it is an emphasis of the first statement, because of the distance between them. This is what al-Zajjaj said.

The second: the first mention refers to his seeing them, and the second refers to his seeing their prostration.

As for His words ﴿prostrating﴾, there are two explanations. The first: it is the prostration known in prayer, but done out of reverence and not as worship.

The second: he saw them humbly submitting, and so he made their submission a prostration, as in the words of the poet:

"... ... ... *** you see the sand hills in it prostrating to the hooves"

It is also said that at the time of this vision he was seventeen years old. Ibn 'Abbas said: he saw this vision on the night of Friday, and it was the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr). When he related it to Ya'qub, Ya'qub feared for him because of the envy of his brothers, so he said: "O my son, this is a dream of the night, and it should not be relied upon." Then, when he was alone with him, ﴿He said: "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot a plot against you. Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy."﴾

As for the naming of him as Yusuf, there are two opinions. The first: that it is a non-Arabic (a'jami) name. The second: that it is an Arabic name derived from al-asaf, and al-asaf in the language means sorrow (al-huzn).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 6:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And thus your Lord will choose you﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: by the goodness of form and character. The second: by abandoning retaliation. The third: by prophethood; this is the saying of al-Hasan.

﴿And will teach you the interpretation of events (ta'wil al-ahadith)﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: the interpretation of dreams; this is the saying of Mujahid. The second: knowledge and wisdom; this is the saying of Ibn Zayd. The third: the outcomes of affairs. From this is the saying of the poet:

For the beloved there are days that remind of them, and for separation, before the day of parting, there is an interpretation (ta'wil).

﴿And will complete His favour upon you﴾. Regarding this there are two aspects. The first: by choosing you for prophethood. The second: by elevating your word and fulfilling your vision; this is the saying of Muqatil.

And there is a third aspect: that He brought your brothers to you, so that He bestowed favour upon them after their wrongdoing towards him.

﴿And upon the family of Ya'qub﴾: by placing prophethood among them.

﴿As He completed it upon your two fathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq﴾. Ikrimah said: His favour upon Ibrahim was that He saved him from the fire, and upon Ishaq that He saved him from the slaughter.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 12, verses 7–10**

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying: ﴿Indeed, in Joseph and his brothers are signs for those who ask.﴾ In these verses there are two interpretations. The first is that they are lessons (ʿibar) for those who take heed. The second is that they are warnings (zawājir) for the God-fearing.

Regarding Joseph and his brothers, there are four opinions. The first is what God, may He be exalted, made manifest concerning the consequences of the transgression against him. The second is the truth of his dream and the soundness of its interpretation (taʾwīl). The third is his self-restraint and his subduing of his desire, until he was preserved from sin and fulfilled the duty of trust. The fourth is relief after the severity of despair.

Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: "No grieving person hears the Chapter of Joseph without finding comfort in it."

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying: ﴿When they said: Joseph and his brother are dearer to our father than we are.﴾ His brother is Benjamin, and the two were full brothers, of one father and one mother. Yaʿqūb had become deeply attached to them both because of the death of their mother, and he increased in showing them care. That was the cause of their envy of them. He loved Joseph intensely, so the envy toward him was greater. Then he saw the dream, and the envy toward him became more intense.

(p-10) ﴿And we are a band (ʿuṣba).﴾ Regarding the ʿuṣba there are four opinions. The first is that it is six or seven men, said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. The second is that it is from ten to fifteen, said by Mujāhid. The third is that it is from ten to forty, said by Qatādah. The fourth is that it is a group, said by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd.

﴿Indeed our father is in clear error.﴾ Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first is that he is in error in his opinion, said by Ibn Zayd. The second is that he is in injustice in his conduct, said by Ibn Kāmil. The third is that he is in manifest love, related by Ibn Jarīr.

They described him as being in clear error for three reasons. The first is that he preferred the younger over the elder. The second is that he preferred the few over the many. The third is that he does not give consideration to what is due to those who look after him.

There is disagreement concerning them: were they adults at that time? Some held that they were adults and believers, and not yet prophets, because they said: ﴿O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners.﴾ This condition can only belong to an adult. Others said: rather, they were not adults, because they said: ﴿Send him with us tomorrow; he will enjoy himself and play.﴾ They sought his forgiveness only after reaching maturity.

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying: ﴿Kill Joseph or cast him out to some land.﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first is: cast him out to some land so that the beasts of prey devour him. The second is: so that he is removed far from his father.

﴿The face of your father will be clear for you, and after him you will be a righteous people.﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first is that they meant the goodness of this world and not the goodness of religion, said by al-Ḥasan. The second is that they meant the goodness of religion through repentance, said by al-Suddī.

It may also bear a third meaning: that they meant the goodness of their circumstances through their father treating them equally, without favoritism or preference.

In this there is evidence that the repentance of a killer is accepted, because God, may He be exalted, did not reject this statement from them.

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying: ﴿A speaker among them said: Do not kill Joseph.﴾ There is disagreement about who among them said this, on three opinions. The first is that he was Rūbīl, who was the eldest of Joseph's brothers and his maternal cousin, said by Qatādah. The second is that he was Shamʿūn, said by Mujāhid. The third is that he was Yahūdhā, said by al-Suddī.

﴿And cast him into the depths of the well (ghayābat al-jubb).﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first is that it means the bottom and deepest part of the well. The second is the darkness of the well in which what is inside is hidden from sight, said by al-Kalbī.

The mouth of the well was narrow and its bottom was wide.

Regarding its being called ﴿ghayābat al-jubb﴾ there are two interpretations. The first is that because his news would be hidden in it. The second is that because his traces would be hidden in it. Ibn Aḥmar said:

(p-12)
Ah, then stay two months, or half a third, until that which has hidden me has hidden my hiding.

Regarding the word al-jubb there are two opinions. The first is that it is the name of a well in Bayt al-Maqdis, said by Qatādah. The second is that it is an unspecified well, and it is only applied to a particular kind of well.

Al-Aʿshā said:

Even if I am in a jubb of eighty cubits in depth, and I am raised by the ladder to the means of the heavens.

Regarding what is called a jubb among wells, there are two opinions. The first is that it is any well that is large, whether or not it contains water. The second is that it is any well that is not lined with stone masonry (lā ṭayy lahu), said by al-Zajjāj, who said: it was called a jubb because it was cut out of the earth by cutting, and nothing was added to it other than the cutting.

﴿Some travelers (al-sayyāra) will pick him up, if you are going to act.﴾ The meaning of yaltaqiṭhu is that he takes him, and from it comes luqṭa (a found object), because it is the lost item that is taken up.

Regarding al-sayyāra there are two opinions. The first is that they are the travelers, so called because they journey. The second is that they are passersby on the road, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The second is that it is from ten to fifteen, said by Mujāhid. The third is that it is from ten to forty, said by Qatādah. The fourth is that it is a group, said by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd.

﴿Indeed our father is in clear error.﴾ Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first is that he is in error in his opinion, said by Ibn Zayd. The second is that he is in injustice in his conduct, said by Ibn Kāmil. The third is that he is in manifest love, related by Ibn Jarīr.

They described him as being in clear error for three reasons. The first is that he preferred the younger over the elder. The second is that he preferred the few over the many. The third is that he does not give consideration to what is due to those who look after him.

There is disagreement concerning them: were they adults at that time? Some held that they were adults and believers, and not yet prophets, because they said: ﴿O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners.﴾ This condition can only belong to an adult. Others said: rather, they were not adults, because they said: ﴿Send him with us tomorrow; he will enjoy himself and play.﴾ They sought his forgiveness only after reaching maturity.

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying: ﴿Kill Joseph or cast him out to some land.﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first is: cast him out to some land so that the beasts of prey devour him. The second is: so that he is removed far from his father.

﴿The face of your father will be clear for you, and after him you will be a righteous people.﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first is that they meant the goodness of this world and not the goodness of religion, said by al-Ḥasan. The second is that they meant the goodness of religion through repentance, said by al-Suddī.

It may also bear a third meaning: that they meant the goodness of their circumstances through their father treating them equally, without favoritism or preference.

In this there is evidence that the repentance of a killer is accepted, because God, may He be exalted, did not reject this statement from them.

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying: ﴿A speaker among them said: Do not kill Joseph.﴾ There is disagreement about who among them said this, on three opinions. The first is that he was Rūbīl, who was the eldest of Joseph's brothers and his maternal cousin, said by Qatādah. The second is that he was Shamʿūn, said by Mujāhid. The third is that he was Yahūdhā, said by al-Suddī.

﴿And cast him into the depths of the well (ghayābat al-jubb).﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first is that it means the bottom and deepest part of the well. The second is the darkness of the well in which what is inside is hidden from sight, said by al-Kalbī.

The mouth of the well was narrow and its bottom was wide.

Regarding its being called ﴿ghayābat al-jubb﴾ there are two interpretations. The first is that because his news would be hidden in it. The second is that because his traces would be hidden in it. Ibn Aḥmar said:

(p-12)
Ah, then stay two months, or half a third, until that which has hidden me has hidden my hiding.

Regarding the word al-jubb there are two opinions. The first is that it is the name of a well in Bayt al-Maqdis, said by Qatādah. The second is that it is an unspecified well, and it is only applied to a particular kind of well.

Al-Aʿshā said:

Even if I am in a jubb of eighty cubits in depth, and I am raised by the ladder to the means of the heavens.

Regarding what is called a jubb among wells, there are two opinions. The first is that it is any well that is large, whether or not it contains water. The second is that it is any well that is not lined with stone masonry (lā ṭayy lahu), said by al-Zajjāj, who said: it was called a jubb because it was cut out of the earth by cutting, and nothing was added to it other than the cutting.

﴿Some travelers (al-sayyāra) will pick him up, if you are going to act.﴾ The meaning of yaltaqiṭhu is that he takes him, and from it comes luqṭa (a found object), because it is the lost item that is taken up.

Regarding al-sayyāra there are two opinions. The first is that they are the travelers, so called because they journey. The second is that they are passersby on the road, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 11–12:

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Send him with us tomorrow, he will enjoy himself and play﴾. Regarding this there are five interpretations. The first: "We will amuse ourselves and play," said by al-Dahhak.

The second: "We will strive and be active," said by Qatadah.

The third: "We will guard one another, and we will amuse ourselves," said by Mujahid.

The fourth: "We will graze and act freely," said by Ibn Zayd, and from it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

Ruha bi-Muslimata al-bighal, muwaddi'an, fa-r'ay Fazara, la hunaka al-mar'a
(The mules have departed with Muslimah, bidding farewell; so graze Fazarah, for there is no pasture over there.)

The fifth: "We will eat and enjoy ourselves," derived from al-ratah (ar-ratʿah), which is abundance of food and drink, said by Ibn Shajarah, and he recited the verse of the poet:

Akufran ba'da radd al-mawti 'anni, wa ba'da 'ata'ika al-mi'ata al-ratta'a?
(Would you be ungrateful after death was turned back from me, and after your giving of a hundred camels, abundant ones?)

That is, the ra'tah, because of the abundance of pasture.

(p-13) Ya'qub, peace be upon him, did not object to them about play, because they meant by it what was permissible.

The Exalted said: ﴿He said, "Indeed, it grieves me that you take him away, and I fear that the wolf will devour him while you are heedless of him."﴾ On this there are two opinions.

The first: he said this out of his fear for him from them, and he meant them by "the wolf," and his fear was only of their killing him. So he referred to them by the wolf, as a figure of speech to avoid addressing them directly. Ibn 'Abbas said: "So he called them wolves."

The second opinion: he feared not them for him, for had he feared them he would not have sent him with them. Rather, he feared the wolf, because it is the most common thing one fears from wild beasts in the open country (al-sahari).

Al-Kalbi said: "Rather, he saw in his dream that a wolf attacked Yusuf, and so he feared it for him."

The Exalted said: ﴿He said, "Indeed, it grieves me that you take him away, and I fear that the wolf will devour him while you are heedless of him."﴾ On this there are two opinions.

The first: he said this out of his fear for him from them, and he meant them by "the wolf," and his fear was only of their killing him. So he referred to them by the wolf, as a figure of speech to avoid addressing them directly. Ibn 'Abbas said: "So he called them wolves."

Al-Kalbi said: "Rather, he saw in his dream that a wolf attacked Yusuf, and so he feared it for him."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 15:

﴿And We inspired him﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

(p-14) First: it means "and We inspired him" in the sense of "and We caused him to receive inspiration (ilham)," as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We inspired to the mother of Moses: "Suckle him"﴾ [al-Qasas: 7].

Second: that God, exalted is He, revealed to him while he was in the well. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

﴿You will surely inform them of this matter of theirs﴾. Regarding this there are two views. First: that He revealed to him that he would meet them and rebuke them for what they had done. According to this view, the revelation came after he was thrown into the well, as good news to him of safety.

Second: that He revealed to him what they were going to do to him. According to this view, the revelation came before he was thrown into the well, as a warning to him.

﴿while they do not perceive﴾. Regarding this there are two views. First: they do not perceive that he is their brother Joseph. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Juraij.

Second: they do not perceive God's revelation to him of prophethood. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 16–18:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They said, "O our father, we went off racing one another"﴾. It is derived from nafta'ila (the reflexive/reciprocal form) from al-sibaq (racing), and in it there are four interpretations. The first: its meaning is "we were shooting arrows at targets (yantasilu) in the race (al-sibaq) of archery," as said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: they meant racing one another on foot.

The third: they meant their racing in the work they were occupied with, namely pasturing and gathering firewood.

The fourth: that is, "we hunt," and that they were racing one another in hunting game.

﴿And we left Joseph by our belongings﴾. It is possible that by leaving him by their belongings they meant to show concern for him, and it is possible that they meant guarding their baggage.

(p-15) ﴿So the wolf devoured him﴾. When they heard their father say, "And I fear that the wolf will devour him," they took that from his mouth and used it as a pretext, because it was the most evident of the dangers to him.

﴿And you would not believe us﴾, that is, you would not accept us as truthful.

﴿Even if we were truthful﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: their saying was not meant to cast doubt on their father's trust in their truthfulness; rather they meant, "Even if we were people of truth, you would not believe us," as said by Ibn Jarir.

The second: its meaning is "even though we were indeed truthful," as said by Ibn Ishaq.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And they came upon his shirt with false blood﴾. Mujahid said: it was the blood of a young goat (sakhlah).

Qatadah said: it was the blood of a gazelle.

Al-Hasan said: when they brought Joseph's shirt, Ya'qub did not see any tear in it, so he said, "O my sons, by God, I have not known the wolf to be gentle: would it devour my son and spare his shirt?"

The meaning of His saying ﴿with false blood﴾ is "blood about which there is falsehood," but He described it with the verbal noun, so its implied sense is "with blood having falsehood."

Al-Hasan recited bi-damin kadhibin with the letter dal unpointed (kadhaba), and its meaning is "with blood that had changed," as said by al-Sha'bi.

In the shirt there are three signs: when they came with the false blood upon it, when it was torn from behind, and when it was cast upon his father's face and he regained his sight.

﴿He said, "Rather, your own souls have made a matter seem good to you"﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: "Rather, your own souls commanded you," as said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: "Rather, your own souls made it seem attractive to you," as said by Qatadah.

In Ya'qub's rejection of them and his denial of them there are three interpretations. The first: that this was by revelation from God, the Exalted, to him after their deed.

(p-16) The second: that he had a prior knowledge of this which God had given him.

The third: that he said this by conjecture, through the correctness of his judgment and the truthfulness of his assumption.

He said, consoling himself, ﴿So patience is fitting﴾. What he commanded his soul of patience admits two interpretations. The first: patience in confronting them for their deed, so this patience would be a pardon of their punishment.

The second: that he commanded his soul to be patient over what he had been tried with, the loss of Joseph.

In His saying ﴿so patience is fitting﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: that it means it is part of what is fitting that I be patient.

The second: that he commanded his soul with fitting patience.

Regarding fitting patience (al-sabr al-jamil) there are two interpretations. The first: that it is the patience in which there is no impatience (jaza').

This was said by Mujahid.

The second: that it is the patience in which there is no complaint.

Habbab ibn Abi Hubla narrated, saying: "The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So patience is fitting﴾, and he said: '(Patience in which there is no complaint, and whoever airs his grief has not been patient.)'" ﴿And God is the One whose help is sought against what you describe﴾. In this there are three interpretations. The first: God is the One whose help is sought for fitting patience.

The second: God is the One whose help is sought to bear what you describe.

The third: that is, against what you lie about, as said by Qatadah.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: God tried Ya'qub in his old age and Joseph in his youth, to see how resolute they both were.

(p-17) His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer﴾, who is the one who goes ahead of them to the water to draw it for them.

The historians mention that he was Malik ibn Dhu'r ibn Hajar ibn Yakah ibn Lakhm.

﴿So he lowered his bucket﴾, meaning he sent it down to fill it. It is said "adlaha" when one sends down the bucket to fill it, and "dallaha" when one brings it up full.

Qatadah said: Yusuf, peace be upon him, clung to the bucket when it was lowered.

The well is at Bayt al-Maqdis, its location being well known.

﴿He said: "O good news! This is a boy"﴾ There are two opinions regarding this. One: he called out to them with the words "good news," announcing to them a boy; this was said by Qatadah. The second: he called out to one of them whose name was Bushra, and he called him by his name to inform him about the boy; this was said by al-Suddi.

﴿And they concealed him as merchandise﴾ There are three interpretations regarding this. One: the brothers of Yusuf were near the well, and when they saw the one who had come to the water bring him up, they said, "This is our slave whom we have seized," then they sold him and kept the sale secret, making his price their merchandise; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: those who came to the well kept the purchase of him secret from the rest of their companions so that it would be their merchandise, so they would not share him with them because of his cheapness; and they agreed among themselves that he was merchandise they had taken for trade from the people of the water; this was said by Mujahid. The third: those who bought him kept the sale secret from the king so that his companions would not learn of it, and they claimed that he was their merchandise.

Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak that he was thrown into the well when he was six years old, and he remained in it until the caravan brought him out, three days later.

Al-Kalbi said: He was thrown into it when he was seventeen years old.

(p-18) His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price﴾. The meaning of "sharawhu" is that they sold him, and from it is the verse of Ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari:

"And I sold a cloak—would that after a cloak I had been a head [of state]."

The term for sale and purchase applies to each of the seller and the buyer, because each of them is a seller of what is in his hand and a buyer of what is in the hand of his companion.

Regarding the seller there are two opinions. One: they were his brothers, who sold him to the caravan when they brought him out of the well, claiming he was a slave; this was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Mujahid. The second: the caravan sold him on behalf of the king of Egypt; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

﴿For a paltry price﴾ There are three interpretations regarding this. One: "bakhs" here means unlawful; this was said by al-Dahhak. Ibn Ata said: because they effected the sale of a person who may not lawfully be sold, so his price, however great, was paltry; and even if his enemies sold him, it is no more wondrous than your selling yourself for an hour's desire of your sins. Two: it means injustice; this was said by Qatadah. Three: it means little; this was said by Mujahid and al-Sha'bi.

﴿Counted dirhams﴾ The amount has been disputed in three statements. One: he was sold for twenty dirhams, which they divided among themselves, and they were ten, so each one of them took two dirhams; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Ata and al-Suddi. The second: for twenty-two dirhams; they were eleven, and each one of them took two dirhams; this was said by Mujahid. The third: for forty dirhams; this was said by Ikrimah and Ibn Ishaq.

Al-Suddi used to say: they bought with them sandals and shoes.

Regarding His words ﴿counted dirhams﴾ there are two interpretations. One: they were counted and not weighed, because of their disregard for him. The second: because they were fewer than forty dirhams, and they did not weigh anything less than forty dirhams, since the least weight among them was the ounce, and an ounce is forty dirhams.

﴿And they were among those who were indifferent to him﴾ Regarding those meant by them there are two opinions. One: they were the brothers of Yusuf, who were indifferent to him when they did what they did to him. The second: the caravan were indifferent to him when they sold him for what they sold him.

Regarding their indifference to him there are two interpretations. One: because they knew he was free and could not be bought. The second: because he was a slave in their possession, and they feared that his owner would find him and take him.

There is also a third interpretation: they were indifferent to his price, testing him and knowing his excellence. Ikrimah said: Yusuf was freed when he was sold.

(p-17) His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿And a caravan came, and they sent their water-drawer﴾, who is the one who goes ahead of them to the water to draw it for them.

The historians mention that he was Malik ibn Dhu'r ibn Hajar ibn Yakah ibn Lakhm.

﴿So he lowered his bucket﴾, meaning he sent it down to fill it. It is said "adlaha" when one sends down the bucket to fill it, and "dallaha" when one brings it up full.

Qatadah said: Yusuf, peace be upon him, clung to the bucket when it was lowered.

The well is at Bayt al-Maqdis, its location being well known.

﴿He said: "O good news! This is a boy"﴾ There are two opinions regarding this. One: he called out to them with the words "good news," announcing to them a boy; this was said by Qatadah. The second: he called out to one of them whose name was Bushra, and he called him by his name to inform him about the boy; this was said by al-Suddi.

﴿And they concealed him as merchandise﴾ There are three interpretations regarding this. One: the brothers of Yusuf were near the well, and when they saw the one who had come to the water bring him up, they said, "This is our slave whom we have seized," then they sold him and kept the sale secret, making his price their merchandise; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: those who came to the well kept the purchase of him secret from the rest of their companions so that it would be their merchandise, so they would not share him with them because of his cheapness; and they agreed among themselves that he was merchandise they had taken for trade from the people of the water; this was said by Mujahid. The third: those who bought him kept the sale secret from the king so that his companions would not learn of it, and they claimed that he was their merchandise.

Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak that he was thrown into the well when he was six years old, and he remained in it until the caravan brought him out, three days later.

Al-Kalbi said: He was thrown into it when he was seventeen years old.

(p-18) His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price﴾. The meaning of "sharawhu" is that they sold him, and from it is the verse of Ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari:

"And I sold a cloak—would that after a cloak I had been a head [of state]."

The term for sale and purchase applies to each of the seller and the buyer, because each of them is a seller of what is in his hand and a buyer of what is in the hand of his companion.

Regarding the seller there are two opinions. One: they were his brothers, who sold him to the caravan when they brought him out of the well, claiming he was a slave; this was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Mujahid. The second: the caravan sold him on behalf of the king of Egypt; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

﴿For a paltry price﴾ There are three interpretations regarding this. One: "bakhs" here means unlawful; this was said by al-Dahhak. Ibn Ata said: because they effected the sale of a person who may not lawfully be sold, so his price, however great, was paltry; and even if his enemies sold him, it is no more wondrous than your selling yourself for an hour's desire of your sins. Two: it means injustice; this was said by Qatadah. Three: it means little; this was said by Mujahid and al-Sha'bi.

﴿Counted dirhams﴾ The amount has been disputed in three statements. One: he was sold for twenty dirhams, which they divided among themselves, and they were ten, so each one of them took two dirhams; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, Ata and al-Suddi. The second: for twenty-two dirhams; they were eleven, and each one of them took two dirhams; this was said by Mujahid. The third: for forty dirhams; this was said by Ikrimah and Ibn Ishaq.

Al-Suddi used to say: they bought with them sandals and shoes.

Regarding His words ﴿counted dirhams﴾ there are two interpretations. One: they were counted and not weighed, because of their disregard for him. The second: because they were fewer than forty dirhams, and they did not weigh anything less than forty dirhams, since the least weight among them was the ounce, and an ounce is forty dirhams.

﴿And they were among those who were indifferent to him﴾ Regarding those meant by them there are two opinions. One: they were the brothers of Yusuf, who were indifferent to him when they did what they did to him. The second: the caravan were indifferent to him when they sold him for what they sold him.

Regarding their indifference to him there are two interpretations. One: because they knew he was free and could not be bought. The second: because he was a slave in their possession, and they feared that his owner would find him and take him.

There is also a third interpretation: they were indifferent to his price, testing him and knowing his excellence. Ikrimah said: Yusuf was freed when he was sold.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah 12, verses 21–22:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And the one who bought him from Egypt said﴾. He was al-'Aziz, its king (malik), and his name was Itfir ibn Ruwayjib.

﴿to his wife﴾. Her name was Ra'il, daughter of Ra'ayil, according to what Ibn Ishaq mentioned.

Ibn 'Abbas said: His name was Qitfir, and he was in charge of the treasuries of Egypt. The king at that time was al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan, from the 'Amaliq.

Muqatil said: The seller who sold him to the king was Malik ibn Du'r, for twenty dinars, and he added to him a garment and a pair of sandals.

﴿Honor his residence﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: beautify his lodging.

(p-20) The second: make his position honorable. Kuthayyir said:

*I wish to stay with her, though I think that if we linger long with her, she grows weary.*

Honoring his residence means (giving him) good food, soft clothing, and preparing a comfortable place for him to sleep.

﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾. It was said: in his price, if we sell him.

It may also mean: he will benefit us in service and in acting on our behalf.

﴿Or we may adopt him as a son﴾, if we free him and take him as our adopted son.

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: The best people in firasa (discernment, insight into character) are three: al-'Aziz regarding Yusuf, when he said to his wife, ﴿Honor his residence; perhaps he will benefit us﴾; the daughter of Shu'ayb regarding Musa, when she said to her father, ﴿O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾ [al-Qasas: 26]; and Abu Bakr, when he appointed 'Umar as his successor.

﴿And thus We established Yusuf in the land﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: by bringing him out of the well. The second: by the king appointing him as his deputy.

﴿And that We may teach him the interpretation of events﴾. We have already mentioned two interpretations of this.

﴿And Allah is predominant over His affair﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: He is predominant over the affair of Yusuf, so that he attains what Allah intends for him. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: He is predominant over His own affair in what He wills, that He says to it, "Be," and it is.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And when he reached his full strength﴾. This means the limit of his strength and the vigor of his youth.

As for al-ashudd (full maturity, the age of full strength), there are six sayings about it:

(p-21) The first: it is the attainment of puberty (bulugh al-hulum). This was said by al-Sha'bi, Rabi'ah, and Zayd ibn Aslam.

The second: eighteen years. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: twenty years. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak.

The fourth: twenty-five years. This was said by Ikrimah.

The fifth: thirty years. This was said by al-Suddi.

The sixth: thirty-three years. This was said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatadah.

This is the beginning of al-ashudd. Regarding its end, there are two sayings. The first: it is forty years. This was said by al-Hasan. The second: it is sixty years, related by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. Suhaym ibn Wuthayl al-Riyahi said:

*A man of fifty, my full strength gathered, and the affairs of life turn me round and round.*

Regarding what is meant by reaching al-ashudd in the case of Yusuf, there are two sayings. The first: twenty years, said by al-Dahhak. The second: thirty years, which is the view of Mujahid.

﴿We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾. Regarding this "judgment" that was given to him, there are five interpretations. The first: intellect, said by Mujahid. The second: judging among people. The third: wisdom in his actions. The fourth: the Qur'an, said by Sufyan. The fifth: prophethood, said by al-Suddi.

Regarding this "knowledge" that was given to him, there are two interpretations. The first: jurisprudence (fiqh), said by Mujahid. The second: prophethood, said by Ibn Abi Najih.

It may also carry a third meaning: knowledge of the interpretation of dreams.

(p-22) ﴿And thus We reward the doers of good﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: the obedient. The second: those who are guided, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The difference between the ḥakīm (one possessing wisdom) and the ʿālim (scholar) is that the ḥakīm is one who acts upon his knowledge, whereas the ʿālim is one who is limited to knowledge without action.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 23:

﴿And she, in whose house he was, sought to seduce him from himself.﴾ She was Ra'il, the wife of al-'Aziz, Idhfir.

Al-Dahhak said: Her name was Zulaykha.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Idhfir, as it has been related to us, was a man who did not approach women, and his wife was beautiful. Yusuf, peace be upon him, had been given a beauty such as no one before him or after him had been given, just as among women there was no one of beauty like Hawwa' (Eve).

Ibn 'Abbas said: Yusuf and Hawwa' shared beauty in halves.

So the wife of al-'Aziz sought to seduce him from himself, summoning him to herself.

﴿And she closed the doors⌝ — regarding this there are two interpretations: One: by multiplying the locks. The second: by multiplying the bolts.

﴿And she said, "Come, you"⌝ — regarding this there are two interpretations: One: its meaning is "I have prepared myself for you." This was said by 'Ikrimah and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, and this is the interpretation of those who read *hayta* with a kasra on the ha' and without the hamza. A poet said:

"Indeed it has troubled me that sleep has silenced them; if it had been meant for them, it would have called out 'hayta'."

The second: "Come here" (halumma laka). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' recited:

"Convey to the Commander of the Faithful, brother of Iraq, when you arrive, that Iraq and its people are a neck toward you, so *hayta hayta*."

This is the interpretation of those who read *hayta laka* with a fatha on the ha', and it is the more correct and more eloquent. Tarafah ibn al-'Abd said:

"My people are not the most distant when a summoner from the clan calls: *hayta*."

Then those who held this interpretation differed regarding the word. 'Atiyyah related from Ibn 'Abbas that *hayta laka* is a word in Coptic whose meaning is "come, for you." Mujahid said rather it is an Arabic word with this meaning. Al-Hasan said: it is a Syriac word.

﴿He said, "I seek refuge in Allah! Indeed, He is my Lord; He has made my dwelling good."⌝ That is: I seek refuge in Allah.

Regarding ﴿Indeed, He is my Lord; He has made my dwelling good﴾ there are two interpretations: One: Indeed Allah is my Lord; He has made my dwelling good, so I will not disobey Him. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: He meant al-'Aziz, Idhfir: "Indeed, he is my lord," that is, my master, "who has made my dwelling good, so I will not betray him." This was said by Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi.

قَوْلُهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿وَلَقَدْ هَمَّتْ بِهِ وهَمَّ بِها لَوْلا أنْ رَأى بُرْهانَ رَبِّهِ﴾ ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord.﴾ As for her desire for him, there are two opinions. The first: it was a desire of lust.

The second: she lay back for him and prepared herself for intercourse with him.

As for his desire for her, there are six opinions:

(p-24) The first: he resolved to strike her when she sought to seduce him, and he did not resolve to have intercourse with her. This was said by some of the later scholars.

The second: the phrase ﴿ولقد همت به﴾ ("And she certainly desired him") is a complete sentence that ends there. Then the report about Yusuf begins: ﴿وَهَمَّ بِها لَوْلا أنْ رَأى بُرْهانَ رَبِّهِ﴾ ("and he would have desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord"). The meaning of the statement is: "Had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have desired her." This was said by Qutrub.

The third: her desire was lust, and his desire was chastity.

The fourth: his desire for her was not a firm resolve and intention, but was only a imagining between acting and refraining. There is no fault in the soul's inner discourse when it is not joined by firm resolve or action. The root meaning of *hamm* (desire/concern) is the soul's inner discourse until it becomes manifest and turns into action. From this is the verse of Jamil:

؎ I resolved upon a resolve concerning Buthayna; had it appeared, I would have cured the burning ailments of love in my heart.

The fifth: his desire was the movement of natural disposition that is in the hearts of men regarding the desire for women, even though he overcame it. This is the meaning of the statement of al-Hasan.

The sixth: he resolved to have intercourse with her and determined upon it.

Ibn Abbas said: "He untied the drawstring (al-himyan, the cord of the trousers)" — meaning the sirwal (trousers) — "and sat between her legs in the position of a man with a woman." This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun).

If it is said: How is it permissible to describe Yusuf with such an act, when he is a Prophet of Allah, Mighty and Majestic? It is said: it was a disobedience from him. Concerning the disobediences of the Prophets there are three aspects.

The first: every Prophet whom Allah tested with a sin, He tested him only so that he would be in awe of Allah, Exalted, whenever he remembered it, and so he would strive harder in obedience out of fear of it, and would not rely upon the vastness of His pardon and mercy.

The second: Allah, Exalted, tested them with that so that He would make them know the value of His blessing upon them by His forgiving them and His not punishing them in the Hereafter for their disobedience.

The third: He tested them with that so that He would make them leaders for the people of sins in hoping for Allah's mercy and not despairing of His pardon for them when they repent.

Regarding His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿لَوْلا أنْ رَأى بُرْهانَ رَبِّهِ﴾ ("had he not seen the proof of his Lord"), there are six opinions. The first: the proof of his Lord that he saw was that he was called to the prohibition of committing the sin. Ibn Abbas said: "He was called, 'O son of Ya'qub, you would commit fornication, so you would be like a bird whose feathers have fallen out, which tries to fly but cannot.'"

The second: he saw the image of Ya'qub, and he was saying: "O Yusuf, will you desire the act of the foolish, while you are written among the Prophets?" Then his lust came out from his fingertips. This was said by Qatada, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

(p-26) Mujahid said: "Each of the sons of Ya'qub was born with twelve males, except Yusuf, who had only two sons born to him, and his offspring was diminished by that lust."

The third: the proof he saw was what Allah, Exalted, had threatened concerning fornication. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "He saw a writing on the wall: ﴿وَلا تَقْرَبُوا الزِّنا إنَّهُ كانَ فاحِشَةً وساءَ سَبِيلا﴾ ('And do not approach fornication. Indeed, it is an immorality and an evil way')" [al-Isra' 17:32].

The fourth: the proof that he saw was the king, Izfir, his master. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The fifth: the proof that he saw was what Allah, Exalted, had given him of the manners of his fathers in chastity, preservation, avoidance of corruption and treachery. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The sixth: the proof that he saw was that, when she desired him and he desired her, he saw a curtain. He said to her: "What is behind this curtain?" She said: "My idol that I worship; I am covering it out of shame before it." He said: "If you are ashamed before what does not hear or see, then I am more worthy that I be ashamed before my God and guard against Him." This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿كَذَلِكَ لِنَصْرِفَ عَنْهُ السُّوءَ والفَحْشاءَ﴾ ("Thus, that We might avert from him evil and immorality") has two aspects. The first: "evil" is lust, and "immorality" is actual sexual contact.

The second: "evil" is the punishment of the mighty king, and "immorality" is committing fornication.

﴿إنَّهُ مِن عِبادِنا المُخْلَصِينَ﴾ ("Indeed, he was among Our chosen servants") — Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read *al-mukhlisin* with a kasra on the lam (المُخْلِصِينَ), and its interpretation is: those who have sincerely devoted themselves to the obedience of Allah, Exalted.

The rest read it with a fatha on the lam (المُخْلَصِينَ), and its interpretation is: those whom Allah has chosen by His message. Yusuf, peace be upon him, possessed both of these qualities, because he was sincere in the obedience of Allah, Exalted, and chosen for the message of Allah.(p-27)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 25–29:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And they both raced to the door﴾, meaning they both hastened toward it. As for Yusuf, he hastened toward it to flee, and as for the wife of al-Aziz, she hastened toward it in pursuit.

﴿And she tore his shirt from the back﴾, because she caught up with him when he had already opened some of the locks, so she pulled him from behind and tore his shirt down to his shin. Ibn Abbas said: it fell off him, and she pursued him.

﴿And they met her lord at the door﴾, meaning they found her husband at the door.

Abu Salih said: "al-sayyid" (the master) is the husband, in the language of the Copts.

﴿She said: What is the recompense for one who intended evil for your family, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?﴾ This is her saying to her husband, to push the suspicion away from herself by casting it upon Yusuf. Had her love been sincere, she would not have done this to him, and she would have preferred him over herself. But it was a desire that had taken hold of her, and a love that had not been purified.

That is because when the intensity of her love was joined with desire, she sought to avert harm by accusing him falsely. Had she been free of desire, she would have sought to avert harm from him by telling the truth.

﴿He said: It was she who sought to seduce me against myself﴾. Because she had cleared herself by lying about him, he needed to clear himself by speaking the truth about her. Had she refrained from lying about him, he would have refrained from speaking the truth about her.

﴿And a witness from her family testified﴾. Because the two had contradicted each other in speech, the king needed a witness by whom he could know which of the two was truthful and which was lying. So a witness from her family testified, meaning a judge from her family gave a ruling, because it was a judgment from him and not a testimony.

There are four opinions concerning it. The first: it was an infant whom God, exalted is He, caused to speak in his cradle. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Dahhak.

The second: it was a creature from among the creatures of God, neither human nor jinn. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: it was a wise man from her family. This was said by Qatada. Al-Suddi said: he was her paternal cousin.

The fourth: it refers to the testimony of the torn shirt. This was also said by Mujahid.

﴿If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is of the liars. But if his shirt is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is of the truthful.﴾ This is because when a man pursues a woman, he is facing her, so a tear in his shirt from the front is evidence of his pursuit. And when he flees from a woman, he is turned away from her, so a tear in his shirt from the back is evidence of his flight.

This is one of the three signs concerning his shirt: the shirt torn from the back was a proof of his truthfulness; and when they brought his shirt stained with false blood; and when it was cast over the face of his father, and he regained his sight.

﴿So when he saw his shirt torn from the back, he said: Indeed it is of your guile; surely your guile is mighty.﴾ By this he knew Yusuf's truthfulness, so he believed him and said: it is of your guile.

Concerning "guile" here there are two views. One: he meant by it her lying about him. Two: he meant the evil to which she had invited him.

Concerning the speaker of this there are two sayings. One: it was the husband, said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq. Two: it was the witness, related by Ali ibn Isa.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Yusuf, turn away from this﴾. Concerning it there are two views. One: turn away from this matter; Qatada said: in a manner of consolation to him regarding the removal of blame. Two: turn away from this statement; said by Ibn Zayd, in a manner of affirming his innocence of the sin.

﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾. This is the saying of the king to his wife, and he is the one who said to Yusuf "turn away from this."

Concerning it there are two sayings. One: he was not jealous, and therefore he remained silent. Two: God, exalted is He, took away his jealousy, and in this was a kindness to Yusuf, so that he was spared her onslaught and overlooked it; so he commanded her to seek forgiveness for her sin, as a repentance from it and a giving up of it.

﴿Indeed you were of the sinners﴾, meaning of the wrongdoers. It is said of one who intended the sin: "khati'a" (he sinned deliberately), and of one who did not intend it: "akhta'a" (he erred). Likewise with "sawb" and "sawab" (right/correct). The poet said:

*By your life, my error and my rightness are upon me, and it is only my wealth that I have destroyed.*

And He said "of the sinners" and did not say "of the sinful women," for the masculine is given precedence over the feminine.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 25–29:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And they both raced to the door﴾, meaning they both hastened toward it. As for Yusuf, he hastened toward it to flee, and as for the wife of al-Aziz, she hastened toward it in pursuit.

﴿And she tore his shirt from the back﴾, because she caught up with him when he had already opened some of the locks, so she pulled him from behind and tore his shirt down to his shin. Ibn Abbas said: it fell off him, and she pursued him.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 30–34:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And women in the city said﴾. Juwaybir said: "They were four: the wife of the chamberlain, the wife of the cupbearer, the wife of the baker, and the wife of the steward."

Muqatil said: "And the wife of the keeper of the prison."

Regarding this "city" there are two opinions. The first: it is Egypt (Misr). The second: it is ʿAyn Shams.

﴿The wife of the ʿAziz is seeking to seduce her young man from himself﴾. They said this to blame her, to criticise her, to establish the innocence of Yusuf, and to deny his sin.

Al-ʿAziz is the title of the king, derived from his might (ʿizzah). From this is the verse of Abu Duʾad:

"A pearl, over which a merchant dived, was brought to the ʿAziz on a day of light rain."

﴿She had been overcome by love﴾, meaning that his love had penetrated to the innermost part of her heart (shaghaf al-qalb).

Concerning *shaghaf al-qalb* there are five opinions:
First: it is the veil of the heart. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.
Second: it is the covering of the heart, a thin white membrane lying over the heart, which is sometimes called the garment of the heart. This was said by al-Suddi and Sufyan.
Third: it is the inner part of the heart. This was said by al-Hasan. It has also been said that it is the core of the heart (habbat al-qalb).
Fourth: it is what lies within the cavity (of the chest). This was said by al-Asmaʿi.
Fifth: it is the terror and alarm that arise from the intensity of love. This was said by Ibrahim.

It is reported among the irregular readings (shadhdh, readings not transmitted in the standard canon), from Ibn Muhaysin, that the verse reads: *qad shaʿafaha ḥubban* (with the letter ʿayn unpointed). Scholars differed about the distinction between the two readings, with two opinions:

[p. 31] First: *shaghaf* with the pointed ghayn means madness, and *shaʿaf* with the unpointed ʿayn means love. This was said by al-Shaʿbi.

Second: *shaghaf* with the dot means deadly love, while *shaʿaf* without the dot is less than that. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Abu Duʾayb said:

"There is no ecstasy except a lesser ecstasy I have found, which has struck the covering of the heart, and the heart is overcome."

﴿Indeed, we see her in clear error﴾. In this there are two meanings. First: in error, deviating from right guidance and turning away from the truth. Second: its meaning is in intense love.

When the intensity of her love was joined with desire, she sought to avert harm from herself by lying about him. And if she had been free of desire, she would have sought to avert harm from him by speaking the truth against herself.

The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿So when she heard of their scheming﴾. In this there are two meanings. First: that it was their blame of her and their denunciation of her. Second: that she had confided her love for him to them, and they spread that news about her.

﴿She sent to them and prepared for them a reclining-place (mutaka)﴾. Regarding *aʿtadat* there are two meanings: first, that it derives from *iʿdad* (preparation); second, that it derives from *ʿudwan* (transgression).

Regarding *al-mutaka* there are three opinions:
First: it is the assembly (majlis). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan.
Second: it is the cushions and pillows on which one reclines. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda and al-Suddi.
Third: it is food, derived from the Arab saying, "We reclined at so-and-so's place," meaning "we ate at his place." The origin is that whoever was invited to a meal was prepared a reclining-place, so food was named *mutaka* by way of metaphor.

On this view, which food is it? There are four opinions:
First: it is citron (al-zumaward). This was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

[p. 32] Second: it is the utrujj (citron). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, and it is the interpretation of those who read it lightened, unhamzated. In their speech *al-matk* means the utrujj. The poet said:

"We drink sin from the cup openly, and we see the citron (*al-matk*) lent among us."

*Al-ithm* means wine, and *al-matk* means the citron.

Third: it is everything that is cut with a knife. This is the view of ʿIkrimah, because it is usually eaten while reclining.

Fourth: it is all food and drink in its general sense. This is the view of Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Qatadah.

﴿And she gave each one of them a knife and said: "Come out before them."﴾ She gave them this outwardly as an aid for eating, but inwardly so that their bewilderment would appear as evidence against them.

Al-Zajjaj said: "He was like her slave, and she would not allow him to go out except by her command."

﴿So when they saw him, they magnified him﴾. In this there are three interpretations:
First: its meaning is that they exalted him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.
Second: its meaning is that they found his state in beauty and loveliness to be great. This was said by Ibn Bahr.
Third: its meaning is that they menstruated at the sight of him. This is an opinion narrated by ʿAbd al-Samad ibn ʿAli al-Hashimi from his father, from his grandfather ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas.

It has also been said that when a woman becomes distressed or frightened, she menstruates, and menstruation is sometimes called *ikbar*. The poet said:

"We approach women in their states of purity, and we do not approach women when they have menstruated, with great menstruation."

[p. 33] ﴿And they cut their hands﴾, out of bewilderment, so that it would be evidence against them concerning what the wife of the ʿAziz had concealed about them.

Regarding the cutting of their hands there are two meanings: first, that they cut their hands until they were severed; second, that they wounded their hands until they bled, from the saying "so-and-so cut his hand" when he wounded it.

﴿And they said: "Far be Allah from imperfection!"﴾ With the alif (*ḥāsha*) in the reading of Abu ʿAmr and Nafiʿ according to the transmission of al-Asmaʿi, while the rest read *ḥāsha lillāh* without the alif. The meaning of both is the same.

Regarding the interpretation of this there are two meanings: first, "God forbid," said by Mujahid; second, its meaning is "Glory be to Allah," said by Ibn Shajarah.

Regarding its origin there are two meanings: first, it derives from the saying "I was in the *ḥashā*" of so-and-so, meaning in his side; second, it derives from the saying "*ḥāshā* so-and-so," meaning "remove him to a *ḥashā*," that is, to a side.

﴿This is not a human being﴾. In this there are two meanings: first, this is not fit for intimacy; second, this is not among the category of human beings.

Regarding this there are two meanings: first, because of what they knew of his chastity, and that if he had been a human he would have obeyed her; second, because of what they witnessed of his excellent beauty and wondrous loveliness. ﴿This is none but a noble angel﴾. It was also read: *mā hādhā bishran* (with a kasra on the bāʾ and the shīn), meaning: "this is not a purchased slave." ﴿This is none but a noble angel﴾, as an exaggeration in preferring him among the category of angels, glorifying his status.

The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿He said: "My Lord, the prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me."﴾ This indicates that she invited him to herself a second time after their circumstances had become apparent, and so he said: "My Lord, the prison is more beloved to me." He means:

[p. 34] Confinement in prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me.

It may bear two meanings: first, that he meant the wife of the ʿAziz in what she invited him to of immorality, and he referred to her with the plural address, either to honour her status in address, or so as to turn from explicit mention to allusion; second, that he meant by this the group of women who cut their hands when they saw him, because of their admiration for him and their winning over of his heart.

﴿And unless You turn away from me their scheming﴾. This may bear two meanings: first, the immorality to which he was invited, if that is attributed to the wife of the ʿAziz; second, the inclination of his heart, if that is attributed to the women.

﴿I might incline toward them﴾. In this there are two meanings: first, "I might follow them," said by Qatadah; second, "I might lean toward them." From this is the verse of the poet:

"Toward Hind my heart has yearned, and Hind is one who stirs yearning like her."
