The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿So when she heard of their scheming﴾. In this there are two meanings. First: that it was their blame of her and their denunciation of her. Second: that she had confided her love for him to them, and they spread that news about her.

﴿She sent to them and prepared for them a reclining-place (mutaka)﴾. Regarding *aʿtadat* there are two meanings: first, that it derives from *iʿdad* (preparation); second, that it derives from *ʿudwan* (transgression).

Regarding *al-mutaka* there are three opinions:
First: it is the assembly (majlis). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan.
Second: it is the cushions and pillows on which one reclines. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda and al-Suddi.
Third: it is food, derived from the Arab saying, "We reclined at so-and-so's place," meaning "we ate at his place." The origin is that whoever was invited to a meal was prepared a reclining-place, so food was named *mutaka* by way of metaphor.

On this view, which food is it? There are four opinions:
First: it is citron (al-zumaward). This was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

[p. 32] Second: it is the utrujj (citron). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, and it is the interpretation of those who read it lightened, unhamzated. In their speech *al-matk* means the utrujj. The poet said:

"We drink sin from the cup openly, and we see the citron (*al-matk*) lent among us."

*Al-ithm* means wine, and *al-matk* means the citron.

Third: it is everything that is cut with a knife. This is the view of ʿIkrimah, because it is usually eaten while reclining.

Fourth: it is all food and drink in its general sense. This is the view of Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Qatadah.

﴿And she gave each one of them a knife and said: "Come out before them."﴾ She gave them this outwardly as an aid for eating, but inwardly so that their bewilderment would appear as evidence against them.

Al-Zajjaj said: "He was like her slave, and she would not allow him to go out except by her command."

﴿So when they saw him, they magnified him﴾. In this there are three interpretations:
First: its meaning is that they exalted him. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.
Second: its meaning is that they found his state in beauty and loveliness to be great. This was said by Ibn Bahr.
Third: its meaning is that they menstruated at the sight of him. This is an opinion narrated by ʿAbd al-Samad ibn ʿAli al-Hashimi from his father, from his grandfather ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas.

It has also been said that when a woman becomes distressed or frightened, she menstruates, and menstruation is sometimes called *ikbar*. The poet said:

"We approach women in their states of purity, and we do not approach women when they have menstruated, with great menstruation."

[p. 33] ﴿And they cut their hands﴾, out of bewilderment, so that it would be evidence against them concerning what the wife of the ʿAziz had concealed about them.

Regarding the cutting of their hands there are two meanings: first, that they cut their hands until they were severed; second, that they wounded their hands until they bled, from the saying "so-and-so cut his hand" when he wounded it.

﴿And they said: "Far be Allah from imperfection!"﴾ With the alif (*ḥāsha*) in the reading of Abu ʿAmr and Nafiʿ according to the transmission of al-Asmaʿi, while the rest read *ḥāsha lillāh* without the alif. The meaning of both is the same.

Regarding the interpretation of this there are two meanings: first, "God forbid," said by Mujahid; second, its meaning is "Glory be to Allah," said by Ibn Shajarah.

Regarding its origin there are two meanings: first, it derives from the saying "I was in the *ḥashā*" of so-and-so, meaning in his side; second, it derives from the saying "*ḥāshā* so-and-so," meaning "remove him to a *ḥashā*," that is, to a side.

﴿This is not a human being﴾. In this there are two meanings: first, this is not fit for intimacy; second, this is not among the category of human beings.

Regarding this there are two meanings: first, because of what they knew of his chastity, and that if he had been a human he would have obeyed her; second, because of what they witnessed of his excellent beauty and wondrous loveliness. ﴿This is none but a noble angel﴾. It was also read: *mā hādhā bishran* (with a kasra on the bāʾ and the shīn), meaning: "this is not a purchased slave." ﴿This is none but a noble angel﴾, as an exaggeration in preferring him among the category of angels, glorifying his status.

The Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿He said: "My Lord, the prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me."﴾ This indicates that she invited him to herself a second time after their circumstances had become apparent, and so he said: "My Lord, the prison is more beloved to me." He means:

[p. 34] Confinement in prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me.

It may bear two meanings: first, that he meant the wife of the ʿAziz in what she invited him to of immorality, and he referred to her with the plural address, either to honour her status in address, or so as to turn from explicit mention to allusion; second, that he meant by this the group of women who cut their hands when they saw him, because of their admiration for him and their winning over of his heart.

﴿And unless You turn away from me their scheming﴾. This may bear two meanings: first, the immorality to which he was invited, if that is attributed to the wife of the ʿAziz; second, the inclination of his heart, if that is attributed to the women.

﴿I might incline toward them﴾. In this there are two meanings: first, "I might follow them," said by Qatadah; second, "I might lean toward them." From this is the verse of the poet:

"Toward Hind my heart has yearned, and Hind is one who stirs yearning like her."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 35:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then it occurred to them, after they had seen the signs﴾. Regarding the signs they had seen, there are two views. The first: the tearing of the shirt and the cutting of the hands.

The second: what appeared to them of his chastity and beauty, so that they said ﴿This is not a human being; this is none but a noble angel﴾ and ﴿They said: "He shall surely be imprisoned until a time"﴾. Regarding "until a time" (ḥīn) there are three views. The first: that ḥīn here means six months, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: that it means seven years, said by Ikrimah.

The third: that it is a time not limited, said by many of the exegetes (mufassirun).

The cause of his imprisonment after the manifestation of his truthfulness is what al-Suddi related: the woman said to her husband, "This Hebrew slave has disgraced me, and claimed that I solicited him. So either you divorce me so that I may make my excuse, or you imprison him just as you imprisoned me." So he imprisoned him.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 12, verse 36:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿And there entered the prison with him two young men.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: One of them was the steward of the king over his food, and the other was the king's cupbearer over his drink. The king, who was the greatest king, al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan, had accused them of poisoning him, so he imprisoned them. Mujahid related that when they were imprisoned with Yusuf, they said to him: "By God, we loved you when we saw you." Yusuf said: "I adjure you by God, if you love me, then no one has loved me without trouble entering upon me because of his love. My aunt loved me, and trouble entered upon me because of her love. Then my father loved me, and trouble entered upon me because of his love. Then the wife of my master, the ʿAziz, loved me, and trouble entered upon me because of her love. I do not want anyone to love me except my Lord."

And it was said: "Young men" (fityan), because they were two slaves, and a slave is called a fata (young man), whether small or great.

﴿One of them said: "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine," and the other said: "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread upon my head, of which the birds eat."﴾ The cause of their saying this, as narrated by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, was that they asked him about his knowledge, and he said: "I interpret dreams." So they asked him about their dreams. Regarding them there are three opinions:

First: they were true dreams that they saw, and they asked him about them. Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq said: "And thus its interpretation came true."

Muhammad ibn Sirin related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The most truthful of you in dreams are the most truthful of you in speech."

Second: they were false dreams, which they asked him about as a test. When he answered them, they said: "We were only playing." He said: ﴿The matter has been decided concerning which you both inquire.﴾ This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn Masʿud and al-Suddi.

Third: that the one who was crucified among them was the liar and the other was the truthful one. This was said by Abu Mijlaz.

His saying ﴿Indeed, I see myself pressing wine﴾ means grapes.

Regarding calling it "wine" (khamr) there are two explanations. First: because its juice becomes wine, so he expressed it by what it will become. Second: the people of Oman call grapes "wine." This was said by al-Dahhak.

Ibn Masʿud recited: "Indeed, I see myself pressing grapes."

﴿Inform us of its interpretation; indeed, we see you are of the good-doers.﴾ Regarding this there are six opinions:

First: they described him thus because he would visit their sick, console their grieving, and widen the space for those among them who were confined. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Second: its meaning is that he would command them to be patient and promise them reward and recompense.

[p. 37]

Third: "Indeed, we see you are among those who excel in knowledge." This was related by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

Fourth: that he would not reject the excuse of one who makes an excuse.

Fifth: that he would fulfill the rights of others and would not fulfill his own rights.

Sixth: "Indeed, we see you are of the good-doers" if you inform us of the interpretation of this dream of ours. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 37–38:

His words, exalted and majestic be He: ﴿He said: "No food will come to you as provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you."﴾ In this there are three opinions.

The first: "No food will come to you as provision in your sleep but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you in waking." This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: "No food will come to you as provision in waking but I will inform you of its interpretation before it reaches you, because he would be told of what is hidden, like Jesus." This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: It was the custom of the king that when he wished to kill a person, he would prepare a specific food for him and send it to him. Joseph disliked interpreting a dream of evil before the person had given up hope, lest it frighten him. So he promised to interpret it when the food reached him. When they pressed him, he interpreted it. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

Likewise, Ibn Sirin related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sees a dream, let him not recount it except to a beloved one or a wise one."

(p-38) ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me,﴾ meaning the interpretation of dreams.

﴿Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah and who are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers.﴾ He turned away from interpreting what they had asked about only because of the honour that was in it for him. He informed them of abandoning the religion of a people who do not believe, as a reminder to them of its certainty and as an encouragement for them to obey Allah.

His words, exalted and majestic be He: ﴿That is from the bounty of Allah upon us and upon the people.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "From the bounty of Allah upon us is that He made us prophets, and upon the people is that He sent us to them as messengers."

It may also bear another meaning: "That is from the bounty of Allah upon us in that He cleared us of fornication, and upon the people in that He delivered them from the sin of slander."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 37–38:

His words, exalted and majestic be He: ﴿He said: "No food will come to you as provision but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you."﴾ In this there are three opinions.

The first: "No food will come to you as provision in your sleep but I will inform you of its interpretation before it comes to you in waking." This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: "No food will come to you as provision in waking but I will inform you of its interpretation before it reaches you, because he would be told of what is hidden, like Jesus." This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: It was the custom of the king that when he wished to kill a person, he would prepare a specific food for him and send it to him. Joseph disliked interpreting a dream of evil before the person had given up hope, lest it frighten him. So he promised to interpret it when the food reached him. When they pressed him, he interpreted it. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

Likewise, Ibn Sirin related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sees a dream, let him not recount it except to a beloved one or a wise one."

(p-38) ﴿That is of what my Lord has taught me,﴾ meaning the interpretation of dreams.

﴿Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah and who are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers.﴾ He turned away from interpreting what they had asked about only because of the honour that was in it for him. He informed them of abandoning the religion of a people who do not believe, as a reminder to them of its certainty and as an encouragement for them to obey Allah.

His words, exalted and majestic be He: ﴿That is from the bounty of Allah upon us and upon the people.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "From the bounty of Allah upon us is that He made us prophets, and upon the people is that He sent us to them as messengers."

It may also bear another meaning: "That is from the bounty of Allah upon us in that He cleared us of fornication, and upon the people in that He delivered them from the sin of slander."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 39–40:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿That is the upright religion﴾ has three possible meanings. The first: "That is the straight religion" (al-din al-mustaqim); this was said by al-Suddi.

The second: "the clear reckoning" (al-hisab al-bayyin); this was said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

The third: it means "the true judgment" (al-qada' al-haqq); this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 39–40:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿That is the upright religion﴾ has three possible meanings. The first: "That is the straight religion" (al-din al-mustaqim); this was said by al-Suddi.

The second: "the clear reckoning" (al-hisab al-bayyin); this was said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

The third: it means "the true judgment" (al-qada' al-haqq); this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 41:

(p-39) His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿O two companions of the prison! As for one of you, he will give his lord (a drink of) wine﴾. And he is the one who said: "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine," so (Yusuf) gave him the good news of deliverance and of his return to pouring wine for his master, because he had been his cupbearer.

﴿As for the other, he will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head﴾. And he is the one who said: "Indeed, I see myself carrying bread upon my head, and birds eating from it." So (Yusuf) warned him of destruction. He was the king's baker. Ibn Jarir said: his name was Mijlath, and the name of the cupbearer was Nabu.

When the one who was doomed heard the interpretation of his dream from the two of them, he said: "We were only playing."

(Allah) said: ﴿The matter has been decided about which you both inquire﴾. In it there are two meanings. One: the question and the answer have been concluded. The second: its interpretation will be fulfilled and will occur.

If it is said: How then did he (Yusuf) state the interpretation of the dream definitively, when for him it is a matter of conjecture through ijtihad, which is not to be asserted definitively? In this there are two answers. One: it is possible that he said it from a revelation from Allah, exalted is He.

The second: because he is a prophet, who asserts with certainty the realization of what Allah, exalted is He, made him utter and caused to pass on his tongue, unlike one who is not a prophet.

The word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And he said to the one of the two whom he thought would be saved, "Mention me before your lord."﴾ On this there are two opinions. The first: it means "to the one who knew he would be saved," so knowledge is expressed with the word "thought." This is the view of Ibn Shajara.

The second: he thought this without certainty.

Regarding his thinking, there are two explanations. The first: because the interpretation of dreams is by conjecture, so he did not state it definitively. This is the view of Qatada.

The second: he was not certain of the truth of the two dreams, so his answer was conjectural because of his doubt about their truth.

(p-40) ﴿"Mention me before your lord"﴾, that is, before your master, meaning the great king, al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan, hoping for deliverance if he mentioned him to him.

﴿But Satan caused him to forget the remembrance of his lord.﴾ On this there are two opinions. The first: the one of the two who was saved, Satan made him forget to mention Yusuf to his master, until the king saw the dream. This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

The second: Yusuf, Satan made him forget the remembrance of his Lord in seeking help from Him and relying upon Him.

Abu Salama narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Yusuf. Had it not been for the word he said, 'Mention me before your lord,' he would not have remained in prison as long as he did."

﴿So he remained in prison for several years (bid' sinin).﴾ Ibn Abbas said: Yusuf was punished with a long imprisonment of several years, because he said to the one of the two who was saved, "Mention me before your lord." Had Yusuf remembered his Lord, He would have delivered him.

Concerning the word "bid'" (a few, an indefinite small number), there are four opinions. The first: from three to seven. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Qutrub.

The second: from three to nine. This was said by Mujahid and al-Asma'i.

The third: from three to ten. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: between three and five. This was related by al-Zajjaj.

Al-Farra' said: "Bid'" is only mentioned with ten and with twenty up to ninety, and it is not mentioned after one hundred.

Concerning the period during which Yusuf remained imprisoned, there are three opinions. The first: seven years. This was said by Ibn Jurayj and Qatada.

The second: he remained twelve years. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: he remained fourteen years. This was said by al-Dahhak, and "bid'" refers only to the duration of the punishment, not the whole period of imprisonment.

(p-41) Wahb said: Yusuf was imprisoned for seven years, and Ayyub remained in affliction for seven years.

Al-Kalbi said: He was imprisoned for seven years after the five years in which he said, "Mention me before your lord."

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 12, verses 43–49:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And the king said, "Indeed, I see seven fat cows"﴾, the verse.

This dream was seen by the great king, al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan, and in it there is gentleness (lutf) from two aspects. The first: it was a means of Yusuf's release from his prison.

The second: it was a warning of a drought, and they took its preparation and readied its provisions.

﴿"O chiefs, explain to me my dream"﴾. That is because when the king did not know the interpretation (ta'wil) of his dream, he proclaimed it among his people so that whoever had knowledge of its interpretation would hear it and explain it to him.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They said, "Confused dreams"﴾. Concerning this there are four views. The first: it means mixtures of dreams; this is the view of Ma'mar and Qatadah.

The second: varieties of dreams; this is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: frightening dreams; this is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: false dreams; this is the view of al-Dahhak.

There is a fifth: dreams of confusion; this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Abu Ubaydah said: al-adghath (confused dreams) are those dreams that have no interpretation, and from this is the saying of the poet:

﴾ Like a bundle of a dream, whose dreamer is dear. ﴿

Hisham narrated from Ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When time draws near, the dream of the believer will hardly be false." Concerning the nearness of time there are two views. The first: it is the equality of night and day, because it is a time of balance in which lights burst forth and fruits ripen, so it was the most truthful time for interpreting dreams.

The second: it is the end of time, at the close of its term.

Al-adghath is the plural of dighth, and the dighth is a bundle of grass gathered together, one part with another. It is also said that it is a handful. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (dighth)﴾. Ibn Muqbil said:

﴾ A gazelle whose bed seems to have been laid with clusters of basil on a northern wind morning. ﴿

Al-ahlam is the plural of hulm, and the hulm is the vision in sleep. Its root meaning is deliberation, and from it comes al-hilm (forbearance), the opposite of frivolity. Thus what is seen in sleep is called hulm, because it is a state of deliberation and calm.

﴿"And we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams"﴾. This shows that the first interpretation, by which dreams are explained, is not the true one that is to be relied upon, because Yusuf gave them the interpretation with truth. Yusuf said to the two young men: ﴿"The matter about which you both inquire has been decided"﴾, because it was a warning of prophethood.

It is possible that God, exalted is He, diverted these people from explaining this dream, as a gentleness toward Yusuf, so that the one of the two who was saved would remember his condition, and the need for him would prompt them to turn to him, and so it would be a cause of his release.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And the one of the two who was saved said, having remembered after a time (ummah)﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: after a period; this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second: after forgetfulness; this is the view of Ikrimah.

The third: after a group (ummah) of people; this is the view of al-Hasan.

Al-Hasan said: Yusuf was thrown into the well at the age of seventeen, and he spent eighty years in slavery, prison and kingship, and his affairs were brought together, and after that he lived twenty-three years.

It is also read as wa-dakara ba'da ummatin with a fatha on the alif and a lightened mim, and al-ummah (with lightening) means forgetfulness.

﴿"I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth"﴾, meaning: I will inform you of the one who has knowledge of its interpretation, but he did not mention it to them.

Ibn Abbas said: the prison was not in the city, so he set off to Yusuf when he was given permission, and that was four years after their separation.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿"Yusuf, O truthful one (al-siddiq), give us interpretation"﴾. The naming of him as al-siddiq (the truthful, one of complete sincerity) admits of two views. The first: for the truth of his interpretation of their two dreams.

The second: for his knowledge of his prophethood.

The difference between al-sadiq (the truthful) and al-siddiq is that the truthful is one whose truth is in his words with his tongue, while the siddiq is one whose truthfulness goes beyond his tongue to the truthfulness of his actions in agreement with his state, so that his inner and outer do not differ. So every siddiq is truthful, but not every truthful person is a siddiq.

﴿"Explain to us concerning seven fat cows"﴾. Qatadah said: they are the years of abundance.

﴿"Which seven lean ones devour"﴾. Qatadah said: they are the years of drought.

﴿"And seven green ears and others dry"﴾. Green means fertility, because the earth is green with its vegetation, and dry means drought, because the earth in it is dry, just as the livestock of fertility are fat and the livestock of drought are lean.

﴿"That I may return to the people"﴾, meaning: so that I may return to the people, who are the king and his people. It is also possible that he meant the king alone, and he expressed him with "the people" as a way of honouring him.

And ﴿"that they may know"﴾, because he hoped that they would know and feared that they would not know, and therefore he said ﴿"that they may know"﴾, meaning its interpretation.

This was not from him a doubt about Yusuf's knowledge, because his knowledge had firmly settled in his soul and he believed him. Rather, he feared one of two matters: either the dream was false, or they might not accept its interpretation, out of their dislike for him, and the matter would be delayed until the time of seeing it with their own eyes.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿He said, "You will sow for seven years in succession (da'ban)"﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: it means consecutive, following one another.

The second: it means the habitual custom in farming.

﴿"And what you reap, leave it in its ear, except a little of what you eat"﴾, meaning: it will come out of its ear, because what is in the ear is stored and not eaten. This statement from him is a command, while the first was a report; and it is permissible, since he was a prophet, that he should command what is beneficial. It is also permissible that the first statement was a command as well, although the more apparent reading of it is that it is a report.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿"Then after that there will come seven hard years"﴾, meaning the years of drought, because of their severity upon their people.

Zayd ibn Aslam related from his father that Yusuf used to prepare food for two people, and he would bring it to a man, who would eat half and leave half. Until one day he brought it to him and he ate all of it. Yusuf said: "This is the first day of the seven hard years."

﴿"They will consume what you have stored up for them"﴾, meaning: you will eat during them what you have saved for them.

﴿"Except a little of what you hoard"﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: what you store, this is the view of Qatadah.

The second: what you store in granaries (husun).

It may also bear a third meaning: except a little of what you sow as seed, because preserving the seed is preserving the food supply.

(p-45) His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿"Then after that there will come a year in which people will be given rain (yughathu)"﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: they will be given relief by the descent of rain; this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second: they will be given relief through fertility; this is related by Ibn Isa.

﴿"And in it they will press"﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations. The first: they will press grapes and olives from the abundance of fruits; this is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: meaning, in it they will bring in livestock from the abundance of pastures; this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The third: they will press the clouds with the descent of rain and abundance of rainfall, from His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"And We sent down from the pressing clouds water pouring forth"﴾ [al-Naba' 78:14]. This is the view of Isa ibn Umar al-Thaqafi.

The fourth: you will be saved (tanjuna), derived from al-'usrah, which is the place of rescue (al-manjah); this is the view of Abu Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj. From this is the saying of the poet:

﴾ Thirsty, seeking help but not helped, and he had indeed been the rescue of the one who was saved. ﴿

The fifth: you will do good and show favour; from this is the saying of the poet:

[p-49] The Exalted's words: ﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾. On this there are three interpretations. The first: it is the statement of the 'Aziz, meaning: "And I do not absolve myself of thinking ill of Joseph."

The second: it leads to accusation when one is in doubt.

﴿Except what my Lord has mercy upon﴾. This admits of two readings. The first: except what my Lord has mercy upon, in that He spares it from evil thinking.

The second: that He restrains it so that it does not act.

This is the interpretation of those who hold that it is the statement of the 'Aziz.

The second interpretation: it is the statement of the wife of the 'Aziz: "And I do not absolve myself, if I did solicit Joseph against himself, because the soul impels to evil when desire overcomes it."

﴿Except what my Lord has mercy upon﴾. This admits of two readings. The first: except what my Lord has mercy upon, of one whom He removes desire from.

The second: except what my Lord has mercy upon, in His subduing of the soul's desire. This is the interpretation of those who hold that it is from the statement of the wife of the 'Aziz.

The third interpretation: it is from the statement of Joseph. Those who hold this have differed about its occasion, in four sayings. The first: when Joseph said, ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, the wife of the 'Aziz said: "Nor when you untied the trousers?" So he said: "And I do not absolve myself; indeed, the soul is a commander to evil." This was related by al-Suddi.

[p-50] The second: when Joseph said that, Gabriel, peace be upon him, nudged him and said: "Nor when you intended?" So he said: ﴿And I do not absolve myself; indeed, the soul is a commander to evil﴾. This was related by Ibn Abbas.

The third: the king who was with Joseph said to him: "Mention what you intended," so he said: ﴿And I do not absolve myself; indeed, the soul is a commander to evil﴾. This was related by Qatadah.

The fourth: when Joseph said ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, the Prophet of God disliked that he might have praised himself, so he said: ﴿And I do not absolve myself; indeed, the soul is a commander to evil﴾. This was related by al-Hasan.

The phrase ﴿ammarah bi-l-su'﴾ (commanding to evil) admits of two readings. The first: it means that the soul inclines toward desire by commanding evil.

The second: that it finds heavy the resolute matters which, if they do not meet firmness, lead to evil.

The Exalted's words: ﴿And the king said: Bring him to me; I will take him for myself﴾. This is the statement of the great king, who, when he knew Joseph's trustworthiness, chose him to take him for himself in special service.

﴿So when he spoke to him, he said: Indeed, today you are with us established and trusted﴾. This is because he inferred from Joseph's speech his intellect, and from his chastity his trustworthiness, so he said: ﴿Indeed, today you are with us established and trusted﴾. This is the rank of the intelligent and chaste person.

On his words ﴿makin﴾ (established) there are two readings. The first: "esteemed (wajih)," as said by Muqatil.

The second: "firmly established in a high rank."

On his words ﴿amin﴾ (trusted) there are three readings. The first: it means "secure (amin), not fearing consequences," as said by Ibn Shajarah.

The second: it means "entrusted (ma'mun), trustworthy," as said by Ibn Isa.

The third: "guardian (hafiz)," as said by Muqatil.

The Exalted's words: ﴿He said: Set me over the treasuries of the land﴾, that is, over the treasuries of your land. On this there are two sayings:

[p-51] The first: this is the statement of some of the over-subtle interpreters (al-mutaʿammiqah), that "the treasuries" here means men, because deeds and words are stored in them, so they became treasuries for them.

The second: this is the statement of the literalists (ashab al-zahir), that they are treasuries of wealth. On this there are two sayings: the first: he asked him for all the treasuries, as said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: he asked him for the granaries of food, as said by Shaybah ibn Na'amah al-Dabbi.

In this is evidence for the permissibility of a person seeking a position for which he is qualified, while he possesses its rights and conditions.

What Ibn Sirin related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab removed me from the administration of Bahrain, then called me back to it, but I refused. He said: 'Why? Joseph asked for an office.'"

If the appointing authority is unjust, people have differed about the permissibility of accepting appointment from him, in two sayings. The first: it is permissible if one acts justly in what one is entrusted with, because Joseph, peace be upon him, was appointed by Pharaoh, and because the consideration in his case is his own action, not the action of others.

The second: it is not permissible for him, because it involves supporting the unjust with aid and legitimizing them by executing their affairs.

[p-51] Those who held this view answered the argument about his appointment by Pharaoh with two replies: the first: Joseph's Pharaoh was righteous; the tyrant was Pharaoh of Moses.

The second: he attended to his property rather than to his actions, so the responsibility for it was removed from him.

The more correct way of generalizing these two sayings is to divide what one takes charge of from the side of the unjust into three categories. The first: what it is permissible for its people to do without exercising independent judgment in its execution, such as alms and zakat. Taking charge of it from the unjust is permissible, because the explicit text specifying its recipients has dispensed with independent judgment in it, and the permissibility of its owners' sole disposal of it has dispensed with executing it.

The second category: what they may not dispose of alone and which requires independent judgment in its disbursement, such as the spoils of fay' (property taken from the enemy without battle). Taking charge of it from the unjust is not permissible, because he would be disposing of it without right, and exercising judgment about what he is not entitled to.

The third category: what its people may take charge of and in which independent judgment has a role, such as judgeships and rulings. The appointment to it is open to qualification. If the function is the execution of a ruling between two consenting parties, or mediation between two compelled parties, it is permissible; if it is enforcing compulsion, it is not permissible.

This is because he inferred from Joseph's speech his intellect, and from his chastity his trustworthiness, so he said: ﴿Indeed, today you are with us established and trusted﴾. This is the rank of the intelligent and chaste person.

On his words ﴿makin﴾ (established) there are two readings. The first: "esteemed (wajih)," as said by Muqatil.

The second: "firmly established in a high rank."

On his words ﴿amin﴾ (trusted) there are three readings. The first: it means "secure (amin), not fearing consequences," as said by Ibn Shajarah.

The second: it means "entrusted (ma'mun), trustworthy," as said by Ibn Isa.

The third: "guardian (hafiz)," as said by Muqatil.

The Exalted's words: ﴿He said: Set me over the treasuries of the land﴾, that is, over the treasuries of your land. On this there are two sayings:

[p-51] The first: this is the statement of some of the over-subtle interpreters (al-mutaʿammiqah), that "the treasuries" here means men, because deeds and words are stored in them, so they became treasuries for them.

The second: this is the statement of the literalists (ashab al-zahir), that they are treasuries of wealth. On this there are two sayings: the first: he asked him for all the treasuries, as said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: he asked him for the granaries of food, as said by Shaybah ibn Na'amah al-Dabbi.

In this is evidence for the permissibility of a person seeking a position for which he is qualified, while he possesses its rights and conditions.

What Ibn Sirin related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab removed me from the administration of Bahrain, then called me back to it, but I refused. He said: 'Why? Joseph asked for an office.'"

If the appointing authority is unjust, people have differed about the permissibility of accepting appointment from him, in two sayings. The first: it is permissible if one acts justly in what one is entrusted with, because Joseph, peace be upon him, was appointed by Pharaoh, and because the consideration in his case is his own action, not the action of others.

The second: it is not permissible for him, because it involves supporting the unjust with aid and legitimizing them by executing their affairs.

[p-51] Those who held this view answered the argument about his appointment by Pharaoh with two replies: the first: Joseph's Pharaoh was righteous; the tyrant was Pharaoh of Moses.

The second: he attended to his property rather than to his actions, so the responsibility for it was removed from him.

The more correct way of generalizing these two sayings is to divide what one takes charge of from the side of the unjust into three categories. The first: what it is permissible for its people to do without exercising independent judgment in its execution, such as alms and zakat. Taking charge of it from the unjust is permissible, because the explicit text specifying its recipients has dispensed with independent judgment in it, and the permissibility of its owners' sole disposal of it has dispensed with executing it.

The second category: what they may not dispose of alone and which requires independent judgment in its disbursement, such as the spoils of fay' (property taken from the enemy without battle). Taking charge of it from the unjust is not permissible, because he would be disposing of it without right, and exercising judgment about what he is not entitled to.

The third category: what its people may take charge of and in which independent judgment has a role, such as judgeships and rulings. The appointment to it is open to qualification. If the function is the execution of a ruling between two consenting parties, or mediation between two compelled parties, it is permissible; if it is enforcing compulsion, it is not permissible.

﴿Indeed, I am a guardian, knowing﴾. On this there are four interpretations. The first: "a guardian of what you have entrusted to me, knowing of what you have put me in charge of," as said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: "a guardian by the writing, knowing by the reckoning," related by Ibn Suraqah, and that he was the first to write on papers (qarratis).

The third: "a guardian by the reckoning, knowing by the languages," as said by al-Ashja' from Sufyan.

The fourth: "a guardian of what you have put me in charge of," as said by Qatadah, "knowing of the years of famine," as said by Shaybah al-Dabbi.

[p-52] In this is evidence that a person may describe himself by the knowledge and merit he possesses. This is not an unrestricted permission for all attributes; rather it is specific to what is connected with a need or relates to an apparent means of gain. It is prohibited in other matters because it involves self-praise and showing off. Had the excellent person refrained from it, it would have been more befitting to his excellence; but Joseph was compelled to it by his circumstances and by what he hoped for, namely gaining mastery over his family.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 56–57:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And thus We established Joseph in the land﴾. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: The Great King, al-Walid ibn al-Rayyan, selected him for the office of Itfir (the minister or chief steward of the king's household) and dismissed him from it.

Mujahid said: And he (al-Walid) embraced Islam at his hand.

Ibn Abbas said: He ruled after a year and a half.

Muqatil narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If Joseph had said: ﴿Indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian﴾, if Allah wills, he would have become king at that very time." Then Itfir died, and the king married him to Itfir's wife, Ra'il. Joseph went in to her and found her a virgin, and she bore him two sons, Ephraim (Afra'im) and Manasseh (Manshah), the two sons of Joseph.

As for the one who claims she was Zulaykha, he said: Joseph did not marry her. When she saw him in his procession she wept, then said: "Praise be to Allah, who made kings slaves through disobedience and made slaves kings through obedience." He took her to himself, and she remained in his household until she died with him, and he never married her.

﴿He settles therein wherever he wills﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: He takes for himself a dwelling in the land of Egypt wherever he wills. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: He does in the world whatever he wills, since the affair has been entrusted to him. This was said by Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

﴿We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will﴾: meaning in this world, with mercy and blessing.

﴿And We do not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾: meaning in the Hereafter, with recompense.

Some interpreters understood it as referring to this world, and some understood it as referring to the Hereafter, and the more sound view is what we have mentioned earlier.

There are two opinions regarding what he was given of this state: The first: It is a reward from Allah, the Exalted, for what He tested him with. The second: He was blessed with it by Allah as a favour from Him, and his reward remains as it is in the Hereafter.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed and were God-fearing﴾. In this there are two opinions: The first: And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believed than the reward of this world, because the reward of the Hereafter is everlasting, while the reward of this world is cut off. The second: And the reward of the Hereafter is better for Joseph than occupying himself with the kingship and luxuries of this world, because of the responsibility that it entails.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the brothers of Joseph came and entered upon him﴾ – the verse.

Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi said: They only came to buy grain from Egypt in the years of famine that Joseph mentioned when interpreting the dream. They entered upon Joseph because he was the one who handled the sale of food, owing to his high rank.

﴿So he recognised them﴾ has two interpretations. The first: he recognised them when they entered upon him without their introducing themselves. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: he did not recognise them until they made themselves known to him, and then he recognised them. This was said by al-Hasan.

It was also said that he recognised them by their Hebrew (ʿibrani) language when they spoke it.

Ibn Abbas said: It was called Hebrew (ʿibraniyyah) because Abraham, peace be upon him, crossed (ʿabara) with them into Palestine, and he settled beyond the river Jordan, so they were called the Hebrews (al-ʿibraniyyah).

﴿But they did not recognise him﴾ because they had parted from him when he was young and he grew up; he was poor and became rich; they sold him as a slave and he became a king. For this reason they did not recognise him, and he did not make himself known to them so that they would recognise him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾. That was because he measured out food for them. Ibn Ishaq said: He loaded for each man among them a camel according to their number.

﴿He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾. Qatadah said: He meant Binyamin, who was Joseph's full brother, from the same father and mother.

Al-Suddi said: He brought them into the house and said, "I have become suspicious of you" – he made himself unrecognisable to them – "so tell me who you are, for I fear that you may be spies." ﴿Do you not see that I give full measure﴾ can have two meanings. The first: he lowered the price for them, so that it became an increase in the measure.

The second: he measured out to them with a full measure.

﴿And I am the best of hosts﴾ has two meanings. The first: that is, the best of those who entertain guests. This was said by Mujahid.

The second, which is also possible: the best of those with whom you have stayed, among the trustworthy. On the first interpretation it is derived from nuzul, which means food; on the second it is derived from manzil, which means house.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me﴾ – meaning in the future, since he had already given them their full measure on this occasion.

﴿And do not come near me﴾, that is, I will not treat you as one who is close to me.

He did not intend that they should keep away from him and not return to him, for by this he was urging them to come back.

Al-Kalbi said: Shim'un was chosen from among them because on the day of the well he was the most eloquent of them in speech and the best in judgement.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: We will seek to persuade (sanurawidu) his father concerning him﴾. Al-murawadah (persuasion/seeking) is striving in the pursuit of something, and it is derived from al-irādah (will, desire).

﴿And we will certainly do it﴾ has two meanings. The first: we will certainly do the persuading of his father and the seeking of him from him.

The second: we will certainly go back to him with their brother. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The first: it is possible that Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to do so as a trial for Jacob, so that his reward would be greatly increased, and he obeyed His command in this.

The second: it is possible that he intended by this to alert Jacob to Joseph's condition.

The third: so that Jacob's joy might be doubled by the return of his two sons to him.

The fourth: so that he might give precedence to the joy of his brother of being reunited with him before his (other) brothers, because of his inclination towards him.

Ibn Abbas said: It was called Hebrew (ʿibraniyyah) because Abraham, peace be upon him, crossed (ʿabara) with them into Palestine, and he settled beyond the river Jordan, so they were called the Hebrews (al-ʿibraniyyah).

﴿He said: Bring me a brother of yours from your father﴾. Qatadah said: He meant Binyamin, who was Joseph's full brother, from the same father and mother.

Al-Suddi said: He brought them into the house and said, "I have become suspicious of you" – he made himself unrecognisable to them – "so tell me who you are, for I fear that you may be spies." The second: he measured out to them with a full measure.

The second: it is possible that he intended by this to alert Jacob to Joseph's condition.

The third: so that Jacob's joy might be doubled by the return of his two sons to him.

The fourth: so that he might give precedence to the joy of his brother of being reunited with him before his (other) brothers, because of his inclination towards him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 63–64:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿So when they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send with us our brother that we may measure [grain]."﴾ They differed concerning the place (nuzul) to which they returned to their father, on two views. The first: [it was] at the wells (al-'arabat) from the land of Palestine.

(p-57) The second: [it was] at the camping-places (al-awlaj) from the direction of the ravine (al-sha'b), below Homs, and he was a man of the desert who had sheep and camels.

﴿They said, "O our father, measure has been withheld from us"﴾, meaning: measure will be withheld from us if we return without our brother, because the king of Egypt bound us to it and demanded him from us, either so that he might see him or so that he might know the truthfulness of what we say from him.

﴿So send with us our brother that we may measure [grain]﴾, meaning: if you send him with us, it will be possible for us to go back to him and measure [grain] from him.

﴿And indeed we will be his guardians﴾, encouraging him to send him with them.

So he did not trust them in that, because of what had happened from them concerning Joseph.

﴿He said, "Shall I entrust him to you except as I entrusted you with his brother before?"﴾, because they had guaranteed to him the protection of Joseph, so they neglected him; therefore he did not trust them concerning what they had guaranteed.

﴿But Allah is the best guardian﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿hafizan﴾, meaning: [the best guardian] among you for your brother.

﴿And He is the most merciful of the merciful﴾. This may have two meanings: first, the most merciful of the merciful in preserving what has been entrusted; second, the most merciful of the merciful regarding what He sees of my grief.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 63–64:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿So when they returned to their father, they said, "O our father, measure has been withheld from us, so send with us our brother that we may measure [grain]."﴾ They differed concerning the place (nuzul) to which they returned to their father, on two views. ﴿And He is the most merciful of the merciful﴾. This may have two meanings: first, the most merciful of the merciful in preserving what has been entrusted; second, the most merciful of the merciful regarding what He sees of my grief.

When they opened their belongings, they found their merchandise had been returned to them. That is, they found the very money they had paid as the price of the food they had obtained.

They said, "O our father, what more could we want? ﴿What more could we want?﴾" There are two interpretations of this:

The first: it is in the form of a question, meaning, "What more could we want after what he has done for us?" This was stated by Qatadah.

The second: its meaning is, "What would we want by lying about what we have told you regarding the king?" This was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

"This our merchandise has been returned to us." This may be their statement to him as an informing, and it may be an encouragement, and the latter is the more apparent of the two possibilities.

"And we will obtain provisions for our family." That is, we will bring them provisions (al-mirah), which is the food one lives on. From this is the verse of the poet:

"I sent you to fetch provisions, and you stayed a year; when will your helper come to the one he helps?"

"And we will obtain provisions for our family." This is a pure encouragement to Jacob.

"And we will guard our brother." And this is an appeal to persuade him.

"And we will gain an extra camel-load." This is an encouragement, and it has two interpretations. The first: the camel-load is what we would carry on it for our brother. The second: a camel-load is the share of our brother, because Yusuf distributed the food among the people, so no one is given more than one camel-load.

"That is an easy measure." This has two interpretations. The first: what we have brought you is a small measure that will not benefit us. The second: what we want is easy for the one who measures for us. This was stated by al-Hasan.

On the first interpretation it is a plea for sympathy, and on the second it is a facilitation.

In this statement of theirs there is also a fulfilment of what Yusuf had sought, in the various ways of persuasion they had employed to draw in their brother, for they had tried to win him over from every direction: by encouragement, by appeal, by plea for sympathy, and by facilitation.

His saying, may He be exalted: "He said, 'I will never send him with you until you give me a solemn covenant in God's name'". There are three interpretations of this covenant. The first: it is their calling upon God as witness against themselves. The second: it is their swearing by God, stated by al-Suddi. The third: it is a guarantor who undertakes responsibility for them, ﴿that you bring him to me unless you are surrounded (by enemies)﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: meaning, unless all of you are destroyed, stated by Mujahid. The second: unless you are overcome in your affair, stated by Qatadah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 67–68:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And he said, "O my sons, do not enter from one gate but enter from different gates."﴾ That is, do not enter Egypt through one gate. In this there are two views. The first: that is, through one of its gates.

﴿And enter from different gates﴾, as said by the majority (al-Jumhur).

The second: through one of its roads.

﴿And enter from different gates﴾, meaning roads, as said by al-Suddi.

Regarding what he feared for them if they entered through one gate, there are two opinions. The first: he feared for them the evil eye (al-ʿayn), because they were people of fine form and beauty, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

The second: he feared that the king would see their number and strength, and would then seize them out of envy or caution, as said by some of the later scholars.

﴿And I could not avail you anything against Allah. Judgment is only for Allah.﴾ That is, I cannot protect you from anything of what I fear for you. So he gave counsel to them at first, and entrusted the matter to Allah at the end.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when they entered from where their father had commanded them, it did not avail them anything against Allah; it was only a need within the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled.﴾ That is, the caution of the creature does not turn back the decree of the Creator.

﴿It was only a need within the soul of Ya'qub, which he fulfilled.﴾ This was the caution of one who is compassionate, and the soul's tranquility through the instruction that they should disperse, out of fear of the evil eye.

﴿And indeed, he was a possessor of knowledge because of what We had taught him.﴾ In this there are three views.

The first: that he was one who acted upon what he knew, as said by Qatadah.

The second: that he was certain of Our promise, which is the meaning of the statement of al-Dahhak.

The third: that he was one who guarded Our instruction, which is the meaning of the statement of al-Kalbi.

The Qur'anic verse "And when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his brother to himself" is glossed by Qatadah: he embraced him and lodged him with himself.

"He said: Indeed, I am your brother" has two interpretations. The first: he informed him that he is Joseph, his brother; this is the view of Ibn Ishaq.

The second: he said to him, "I am your brother in place of your brother who was lost"; this is the view of Wahb.

"So do not be distressed by what they used to do" has two interpretations. The first: "Do not grieve," this is the view of Ibn Bahr.

The second: "Do not grieve by what they used to do."

Regarding this (phrase) there are two interpretations. The first: by what they did in the past to you and your brother.

The second: by their taking exclusive control, without you, of your father's wealth.(p-61)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 70–72:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So when he had furnished them with their provisions﴾, which is the measuring out of food for them after their honouring and his giving them a camel-load for their brother, the same as what he had given them.

﴿He put the drinking-cup (al-siqayah) in his brother's bag﴾. Al-siqayah and al-suwa' are one and the same.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Every vessel that is drunk from is a suwa'." The poet said:

"We drink wine openly from the suwa', and we see the flagon (al-matk) lent among us."

Qatadah said: "It was the vessel of the matk (flagon) from which it was drunk."

Its substance was disputed. 'Ikrimah said it was of silver. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said it was of gold, and with it he (Yusuf) measured their food, as an exaggeration in honouring them.

Al-Suddi said: it was the standard measuring bowl (al-makkuk al-'adi) whose two ends meet.

﴿Then a caller called out: "O caravan, indeed you are thieves!"﴾ That is, a caller proclaimed. The proclamation was named adhan (call) because it is an announcement, like the adhan.

Regarding ﴿al-'ir﴾ (the caravan) there are two views. One: it is the company of travellers. Two: it is the laden camels that are ridden, as said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

If it is asked: how did Yusuf permit himself to put the drinking-cup in his brother's bag, so as to make them appear thieves when they were innocent? This is a sin. It is answered with four responses. First: it was a sin committed by the one who measured, and Yusuf did not order it. Second: the caller who measured at the time the cup was missed thought that they had stolen it, and he did not know what Yusuf had done, so he was not sinning. Third: the proclamation was by Yusuf's order, and by it he meant their theft of Yusuf from his father, and that is true. Fourth: it was a fault on Yusuf's part, for which God punished him by the people saying ﴿If he steals, a brother of his stole before﴾, meaning Yusuf.

Some of those who speak of subtle meanings went to the view that the meaning of His words ﴿Indeed, you are thieves﴾ is: indeed you are disobedient to your father concerning your brother, since you took him from him and betrayed him in that matter.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿They said, while turning towards them: "What is it that you are missing?"﴾ Because they denied what they were accused of, while confident in themselves, so they asked in the manner of one astonished.

﴿They said: "We are missing the king's suwa'."﴾ The suwa' is one. Ghalib al-Laythi related from Yahya ibn Ya'mur that he used to recite ṣawgh (ṣawgh al-malik) with a dotted ghayn, derived from al-siyagha (goldsmithing), because it is wrought (maṣwugh) of silver or gold, and it is said of copper.

﴿And for whoever brings it, there is the load of a camel, and I am its guarantor (za'im)﴾. This is a ju'alah (reward) offered to the one who finds it.

Regarding the load of a camel there are two views. One: the load of a camel, which is the view of the majority. Two: the load of a donkey, which is a dialect form, as said by Mujahid.

This offer has been disputed on two views. One: the caller offered it on his own behalf, because he said ﴿and I am its guarantor﴾, that is, a surety who is responsible.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 73–76:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They said, "By God, you know that we did not come to cause corruption in the land."﴾ That is, to steal, because theft is a form of corruption in the land.

They said this to them because they had known them to be upright and chaste.

It was also said that they said this because they had returned the merchandise they had found in their saddlebags, and whoever returns a trust in the absence of its owner would not proceed to steal property in his presence.

﴿And we were not thieves.﴾ This may have two meanings. The first: we were not thieves of others, so that we would steal from you. The second: we were not thieves of your trust, so that we would steal something other than your trust.

The second is more likely, because by this they attributed to themselves an act (of honesty).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They said, "What is the penalty for it, if you are lying?"﴾ That is, what is the punishment for whoever among you steals, if you are lying in claiming that you did not steal from us?

﴿They said, "Its penalty is that he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself is its penalty."﴾ That is, the penalty for the thief is that he be enslaved (istirqaq).

﴿Thus do We requite the wrongdoers.﴾ That is, thus do We deal with wrongdoers when they steal. And this was from the religion of Ya'qub (Jacob).

﴿So he began with their bags before the bag of his brother﴾ so that suspicion would be removed from their hearts had he begun with his brother's bag.

﴿Then he extracted it from his brother's bag.﴾ It was said that it refers to the drinking-cup (al-siqaya), and therefore it is feminine (unnathat, the feminine form is used). It was also said that it refers to the measure (al-sa'), and it is used in both the masculine (yudhakkar) and the feminine (yu'annath) forms, according to the saying of al-Zajjaj.

(p. 64) ﴿Thus did We contrive for Yusuf.﴾ In this there are two meanings. The first: We devised for Yusuf. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: We planned for Yusuf. This was said by Ibn Eesa.

﴿He could not have taken his brother under the religion of the king.﴾ In this there are three meanings. The first: under the authority of the king. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: under the judgment of the king. This was said by Qatada.

The third: under the custom of the king. Ibn Eesa said: and under the religion of the king there was no enslaving of whoever stole.

Al-Dahhak said: rather, the penalty imposed upon him was multiplied.

﴿Unless God wills.﴾ In this there are two meanings. The first: unless God wills that whoever stole be enslaved. The second: unless God wills to grant Yusuf an excuse for what he did.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 77:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿They said, "If he steals, then a brother of his has stolen before."﴾ They mean Yusuf.

In this statement of theirs there are two aspects. The first: it was a punishment upon Yusuf, which Allah, the Exalted, caused to pass through their tongues. This was said by Ikrimah.

The second: they wished to disassociate themselves from his act, because he was not from their mother, and that if he stole, then the root of his brother, the thief, had pulled him along, for sharing in lineage entails a similarity in character.

As for the theft with which they attributed Yusuf: there are five opinions. The first: he stole an idol belonging to his maternal grandfather, made of silver and gold, broke it, and threw it on the road, so they reproached him for that. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah.

(p-65) The second: he was with his brothers at a meal, and he looked at a bone, and hid it, so they reproached him for that. This was said by Atiyyah al-Awfi.

The third: he used to steal from the food of the table for the poor. This was related by Ibn Isa.

The fourth: his paternal aunt, who was the eldest of Ishaq's children, and to whom the girdle (mintaqah) of Ishaq passed because it was with the eldest of his offspring, and who was looking after Yusuf. When Ya'qub wished to take him from her, she placed the girdle upon him, accused him, and took it from him; thus she became, in their judgment, more entitled to him. That was from her out of her intense inclination and love for him. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: they lied about him in what they attributed to him. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿So Yusuf concealed it within himself and did not reveal it to them﴾. In this there are two aspects. The first: he concealed within himself their saying, ﴿"If he steals, then a brother of his has stolen before."﴾ This was said by Ibn Shajarah and Ali ibn Isa.

The second: he concealed within himself ﴿"You are worse in position"﴾, to the end of the verse. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Ishaq.

As for His saying, ﴿"You are worse in position"﴾, there are two aspects. The first: you are worse in rank with Allah than the one you have attributed to this theft.

The second: you are worse in conduct for what you have undertaken of wronging your brother and disobeying your father.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"And Allah knows best what you describe"﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: what you say. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: what you lie about. This was said by Qatadah.

Some of the exegetes have related that when they entered upon him, he called for the drinking cup (suwa'), struck it, then brought it near his ear, and said: "Indeed this cup of mine informs me that you were twelve men, and that you took away a brother of yours and sold him." When Binyamin heard this, he stood, prostrated to Yusuf, and said: "O King, ask this cup of yours about my brother: is he alive or dead?" So he struck it, then said: "He is alive, and you will see him."

He (Binyamin) said: "Do with me whatever you wish, for if he knows about me, he will rescue me."

He said: Yusuf entered, wept, then performed ablution and came out. Binyamin said: "Strike your cup so that it may inform you about the one who stole it." So he placed it in my saddlebag, and he struck it, and said:

(p-66) "This cup of mine is angry, and it says: 'How do you ask me about my companion, when you have seen with whom I was?'"

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 78–79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Chief of the land, indeed he has an aged father﴾. However, they said that for the sake of softening and seeking his compassion. In their saying ﴿aged﴾ there are two meanings. One: aged in years. The second: great in standing, because advanced age is known from the condition of an elder.

﴿So take one of us in his place﴾, meaning, as a slave in his stead.

﴿Indeed, we see you to be among the doers of good﴾. In this there are two meanings. One: we see you as among the doers of good in this matter, if you do it. This was said by Ibn Ishaq. The second: we see you as among the doers of good in what you have been doing with us, by honoring us and giving full measure and our merchandise.

And it may carry a third meaning: indeed we see you as among the just, because the just is a doer of good.

Yusuf answered them concerning this: ﴿He said, "We seek refuge in Allah that we take except him with whom we found our property. Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers"﴾, if we were to seize an innocent man in place of the guilty. In it there is a second meaning: indeed we would then be wrongdoers in your sight, if we judged against you by other than the judgment of your father, that whoever steals is enslaved.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 78–79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Chief of the land, indeed he has an aged father﴾. However, they said that for the sake of softening and seeking his compassion. In their saying ﴿aged﴾ there are two meanings. One: aged in years. The second: great in standing, because advanced age is known from the condition of an elder.

The second: we see you as among the doers of good in what you have been doing with us, by honoring us and giving full measure and our merchandise.

Indeed, we would then be wrongdoers"﴾, if we were to seize an innocent man in place of the guilty. In it there is a second meaning: indeed we would then be wrongdoers in your sight, if we judged against you by other than the judgment of your father, that whoever steals is enslaved.

The Exalted said: ﴿So when they had despaired of him﴾, meaning they despaired of their brother being returned to them.

Second opinion: they were certain that he would not be returned to them. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, who recited the verse of the poet:

؎ I say to her in the ravine, when they capture me: "Did you not despair that I am the son of Faris Zahdam?"

﴿They withdrew apart, conferring privately﴾, meaning some of them withdrew with others, conferring together and consulting, with no one else mixed in among them.

﴿Said their eldest﴾. There are three views on this. The first is that he meant the eldest in intellect and knowledge, who was Shim'un, the one who had kept Yusuf as a pledge with him when his brothers returned to their father. This was said by Mujahid.

The second is that he meant the eldest in age, who was Ruwbil, the son of Yusuf's maternal aunt. This was said by Qatada.

The third is that he meant the eldest in judgment and discernment, who was Yahudha. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿Do you not know that your father has taken an oath from you in God's name﴾, meaning at the time he sent this son of his with you.

﴿And before this, you failed in regard to Yusuf﴾, meaning you neglected him.

﴿So I will not leave this land﴾, meaning the land of Egypt.

﴿Until my father permits me﴾, meaning to return.

﴿Or God decides for me, and He is the best of judges﴾. There are two views on this. One is that it means: or God decrees for me my departure from it. This is the view of the majority.

The second is: or God decides for me by the sword and by fighting, because they had resolved upon that. This was said by Abu Salih.

The Exalted said: ﴿Return to your father and say: "O our father, indeed your son has stolen"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas read (سُرِقَ) with a damma on the sin and a kasra on the ra' and with shadda.

﴿And we bore witness only to what we knew﴾. There are two views on this. The first: we did not bear witness before you that your son had stolen except by what we knew of the presence of the theft in his baggage. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

The second: we did not bear witness before Yusuf that the thief is enslaved except by what we knew of your religion. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿And we were not guardians of the unseen﴾. There are two views on this. The first: we did not know that your son would steal. This was said by Qatada.

The root of haradh (حَرَضٌ) is the corruption of the body and mind due to illness or passion. Al-Arji said:

I am a man whom love has obstinately seized, and it wore me down,
until I was worn out, and until sickness wasted me.

﴿Or become one of the perishing﴾, meaning dead among the dead. All of them said this.

If it is asked: how did Joseph remain apart from his father after he became a king firmly established in Egypt, while his father was in Harran, in the land of al-Jazirah? Why did he not hasten to summon him, and did not make excuses one after another? It is said that four explanations are possible. The first: he did that by the command of God, the Exalted, as a trial for him, for a benefit He knew in it, because he was a prophet who was commanded.

The second: he was afflicted with imprisonment, so after his separation he wished to test himself with patience.

The third: in the sudden arrival of joy there is danger, so he wished to train himself gradually.

The fourth: so that the Great King would not imagine the destitution of his family by hastening to summon them at the time he took power.

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He said, "I only complain of my anguish and my sorrow to God"﴾. Regarding bathth (بَثِّي) there are two interpretations. The first: my worry, said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: my need, related by Ibn Jarir.

Al-bathth (الْبَثُّ) is the scattering of worry by revealing what is in the soul.

He complained of what was in himself, and called it bathth, though it was mabthuth (مَبْثُوثٌ), that is, scattered.

﴿And I know from God what you do not know﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: I know that Joseph's dream is true, and that I will prostrate to him, said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: his soul sensed something when they informed him, so he summoned the king and said, "Perhaps it is Joseph," and said, "There is no truthful one on earth except a prophet," said by al-Suddi.

The reason for Ya'qub's saying ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my sorrow to God﴾ is what is related: a man entered upon him and said, "What has brought you to what I see?" He said, "The long duration of time and the abundance of sorrows."

So God revealed to him: "O Ya'qub, do you complain about Me?" He said: "A sin that I committed; so forgive it for me."

And after that he would say: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my sorrow to God﴾.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Go and seek out news of Joseph and his brother﴾. *Ay* means "that is": *istaʿlimū* (seek information) and *taʿarrafū* (find out). From the same root is the verse of ʿAdiyy ibn Zayd:

*"If you live, I will not seek news of you in my land,*
*and if you fall ill, do not let my visitors seek news of you."*

The root *ḥ-s-s* originally means seeking something through the senses (*ḥiss*).

﴿And do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾. There are two interpretations. The first: "of the relief from Allah," said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq. The second: "of the mercy of Allah," said by Qatadah.

The word *rawḥ* is derived from *rīḥ*, the wind that brings benefit.

Yaʿqub said this because he had perceived, regarding Joseph, the return of the merchandise, the detention of his brother, and the display of honour. It is also reported that Yaʿqub asked the Angel of Death: "Have you taken the spirit of Joseph?" He replied: "No."

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿When they entered upon him, they said: O 'Azīz, adversity has touched us and our family﴾. This is the most gentle appeal and the most eloquent plea for compassion.

There are two views on their purpose in saying this. The first: that he would return their brother to them, said by Ibn Jarir. The second: that he would give them full measure and show them favour, said by ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

﴿And we have come with meagre merchandise﴾. The root of *ijāʾ* is driving with a push. On this there is the verse of the poet ʿAdiyy ibn al-Riqaʿ:

*"He drives a thick-necked camel whose horn's tip*
*is like a pen that has taken its ink from the inkwell."*

There are five views on what this merchandise was:
First: that it was dirhams, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.
(p-73) Second: the goods of the Bedouins, wool and clarified butter, said by ʿAbdullah ibn al-Harith.
Third: the green seed and pine nuts, said by Abu Salih.
Fourth: roasted barley flour (*sawīq*), said by al-Dahhak.
Fifth: worn ropes and sacks, also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas.

On *al-muzjāh* (meagre) there are three interpretations:
First: that it is inferior, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.
Second: that it is unsaleable, said by al-Dahhak.
Third: that it is scant, said by Mujahid.

Ibn Ishaq said: it is that which does not reach the measure of need. From the same usage is the verse of al-Ra'i:

*"And [I sent] a messenger who is not suspected,*
*and a need that is not meagre among the pilgrims."*

Al-Kalbi said it is a word from the language of non-Arabs, and al-Haytami said it is from the language of the Copts.

*and appoint al-Ashʿari over us for nights."*

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 89–92:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Said he, "Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother?"﴾ The meaning of His saying ﴿Do you know what you did﴾ is: indeed you know, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾, meaning: indeed there has come.

Ibn Ishaq said: It was related to us that when they said, ﴿Adversity has touched us and our family﴾, he had mercy on them and was softened toward them, so he said, "Do you know what you did with Joseph and his brother?" And he enumerated for them what they had done to the two of them.

﴿When you were ignorant﴾. There are three interpretations of this. First: it means the ignorance of youth. Second: the ignorance of sins. Third: ignorance of the consequences of their actions.

Then they recognized him.

﴿They said, "Are you indeed Joseph?" He said, "I am Joseph, and this is my brother."﴾ Al-Dahhak related, in the recitation (qira'a, the manner of reciting the text) of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "and this is my brother, and between me and him is kinship." ﴿Allah has certainly favored us.﴾ That is, with safety, and then with honor. It may also mean by reunion after long separation.

﴿Indeed, he who fears Allah and is patient﴾. There are two views on this. One: he who guards against fornication and is patient in remaining unmarried; this was said by Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i).

Second: he who fears Allah, exalted is He, and is patient under His trial.

This is a possible reading.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good.﴾ There are two views on this. One: in this world. Two: in the Hereafter.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They said, "By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us.﴾ It is derived from preference (iithar), which is the intention to prefer one of two souls over the other. The poet said:

"Allah named you with a blessed name, and Allah preferred you with that preference."

﴿And we were indeed sinners﴾, that is, regarding what they did to Joseph. There are two views on this. One: sinful. Two: mistaken. The difference between the sinner (khati') and the one who errs (mukhti') is that the sinner is culpable.

If it is said: They were children at the time of their deed, and sins are lifted from children.

It is said: When they grew up and continued to conceal what they had done, they then became sinners.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿He said, "No reproach upon you today.﴾ There are two statements, with four interpretations. One: "No change (of attitude) against you," this is the saying of Sufyan ibn Uyayna. Two: "No rebuke for what you did," said by Ibn Ishaq. Three: "No refusal against you in what you say," said by Mujahid. Four: "No punishment against you." The poet said:

"So I pardoned them with a pardon that does not reproach, and I left them to the punishment of an everlasting day."

﴿May Allah forgive you today﴾ may have two meanings. One: for their repentance through acknowledgment and regret. Two: for his granting them release by pardoning them.

﴿And He is the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ may have two meanings. One: in His dealing with me when He made me a king. Two: in His pardoning you for what of your sins preceded.

قَوْلُهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿اذْهَبُوا بِقَمِيصِي هَذا فَألْقُوهُ عَلى وجْهِ أبِي يَأْتِ بَصِيرًا﴾ وفِيهِ وجْهانِ: أحَدُهُما: مُسْتَبْصِرًا بِأمْرِي لِأنَّهُ إذا شَمَّ رِيحَ القَمِيصِ عَرَفَنِي.

الثّانِي: بَصِيرًا مِنَ العَمى فَذاكَ مِن أحَدِ الآياتِ الثَّلاثِ في قَمِيصِ يُوسُفَ بَعْدَ الدَّمِ الكَذِبِ وقَدِّهِ مِن دُبُرِهِ.

وَفِيهِ وجْهٌ آخَرُ لِأنَّهُ قَمِيصُ إبْراهِيمَ أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الجَنَّةِ لَمّا أُلْقِيَ في النّارِ، فَصارَ لِإسْحاقَ ثُمَّ لِيَعْقُوبَ، ثُمَّ لِيُوسُفَ فَخُلِّصَ بِهِ مِنَ الجُبِّ وحازَهُ حَتّى ألْقاهُ أخُوهُ عَلى وجْهِ أبِيهِ فارْتَدَّ بَصِيرًا، ولَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِما سَبَقَ مِن سَلامَةِ إبْراهِيمَ مِنَ النّارِ ويُوسُفَ مِنَ الجُبِّ أنَّ يَعْقُوبَ يَرْجِعُ بِهِ بَصِيرًا.

قالَ الحَسَنُ: لَوْلا أنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى أعْلَمَ يُوسُفَ بِذَلِكَ لَمْ يَعْلَمْ أنَّهُ يَرْجِعُ إلَيْهِ بَصَرُهُ وكانَ الَّذِي حَمَلَ قَمِيصَهُ يَهُوذا بْنُ يَعْقُوبَ، قالَ لِيُوسُفَ: أنا الَّذِي حَمَلْتُ إلَيْهِ قَمِيصَكَ بِدَمٍ كَذِبٍ فَأحْزَنْتُهُ فَأنا الآنَ أحْمِلُ قَمِيصَكَ لِأُسِرَّهُ ولِيَعُودَ إلَيْهِ بَصَرُهُ فَحَمَلَهُ، حَكاهُ السُّدِّيُّ.

﴿وَأْتُونِي بِأهْلِكم أجْمَعِينَ﴾ لِتَتَّخِذُوا مِصْرَ دارًا.

قالَ مَسْرُوقٌ: فَكانُوا ثَلاثَةً وتِسْعِينَ بَيْنَ رَجُلٍ وامْرَأةٍ.
