قَوْلُهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿وَلَمّا فَصَلَتِ العِيرُ﴾ أيْ خَرَجَتْ مِن مِصْرَ مُنْطَلِقَةً إلى الشّامِ.

﴿قالَ أبُوهم إنِّي لأجِدُ رِيحَ يُوسُفَ﴾ فِيها قَوْلانِ: أحَدُهُما: أنَّها أماراتٌ شاهِدَةٌ وعَلاماتٌ قَوِيَ ظَنُّهُ بِها، فَكانَتْ هي الرِّيحُ الَّتِي

(p-٧٧)وَجَدَها لِيُوسُفَ، مَأْخُوذٌ مِن قَوْلِهِمْ تَنَسَّمْتَ رائِحَةَ كَذا وكَذا إذا قَرُبَ مِنكَ ما ظَنَنْتَ أنَّهُ سَيَكُونُ.

والقَوْلُ الثّانِي: وهو قَوْلُ الجُمْهُورِ أنَّهُ شَمَّ رِيحَ يُوسُفَ الَّتِي عَرَفَها.

قالَ جَعْفَرُ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: وهي رِيحُ الصَّبا.

ثُمَّ اعْتَذَرَ فَقالَ: ﴿لَوْلا أنْ تُفَنِّدُونِ﴾ فِيهِ أرْبَعَةُ أقاوِيلَ: أحَدُها: لَوْلا أنْ تُسَفِّهُونِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ ومُجاهِدٌ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ النّابِغَةِ الذُّبْيانِيِّ:

إلّا سُلَيْمانَ إذْ قالَ المَلِيكُ لَهُ * قُمْ في البَرِيَّةِ فاجْدُدْها عَنِ الفَنَدِ

أيْ عَنِ السَّفَهِ.

الثّانِي: مَعْناهُ لَوْلا أنْ تُكَذِّبُونِ، قالَهُ سَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ والضَّحّاكُ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ الشّاعِرِ:

هَلْ في افْتِخارِ الكَرِيمِ مِن أوَدٍ * أمْ هَلْ لِقَوْلِ الصَّدِيقِ مِن فَنَدِ

أيْ مِن كَذِبٍ.

الثّالِثُ: لَوْلا أنْ تُضَعِّفُونِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ إسْحاقَ.

والتَّفْنِيدُ: تَضْعِيفُ الرَّأْيِ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ الشّاعِرِ:

يا صاحِبَيَّ دَعا لَوْمِي وتَفْنِيدِي * فَلَيْسَ ما فاتَ مِن أمْرِي بِمَرْدُودِ

وَكانَ قَوْلُ هَذا لِأوْلادِ بَنِيهِ، لِغَيْبَةِ بَنِيهِ عَنْهُ، فَدَلَّ هَذا عَلى أنَّ الجَدَّ أبٌ.

الرّابِعُ: لَوْلا أنْ تَلُومُونِي، قالَهُ ابْنُ بَحْرٍ.

وَمِنهُ قَوْلُ جَرِيرٍ:

يا عاذِلَيَّ دَعا المَلامَةَ واقْصِرا * طالَ الهَوى وأطَلْتُما التَّفْنِيدا

واخْتَلَفُوا في المَسافَةِ الَّتِي وجَدَ رِيحَ قَمِيصِهِ مِنها عَلى ثَلاثَةِ أقاوِيلَ: أحَدُها: أنَّهُ وجَدَها مِن مَسافَةِ عَشَرَةِ أيّامٍ.

قالَهُ أبُو الهُذَيْلِ.

(p-٧٨)الثّانِي: مِن مَسِيرَةِ ثَمانِيَةِ أيّامٍ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ.

الثّالِثُ: مِن مَسِيرَةِ سِتَّةِ أيّامٍ، قالَهُ مُجاهِدٌ.

وَكانَ يَعْقُوبُ بِأرْضِ كَنْعانَ ويُوسُفُ بِمِصْرَ وبَيْنَهُما ثَمانُونَ فَرْسَخًا (الفَرْسَخُ: وحْدَةُ مَسافَةٍ قَدِيمَةٌ تُقَدَّرُ بِنَحْوِ ثَلاثَةِ أمْيالٍ)، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ.

قَوْلُهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ: ﴿قالُوا تاللَّهِ إنَّكَ لَفي ضَلالِكَ القَدِيمِ﴾ فِيهِ أرْبَعَةُ تَأْوِيلاتٍ: أحَدُها: أيْ في خَطَئِكَ القَدِيمِ، قالَهُ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ وابْنُ زَيْدٍ.

الثّانِي: في جُنُونِكَ القَدِيمِ، قالَهُ سَعِيدُ بْنُ جُبَيْرٍ.

قالَ الحَسَنُ: وهَذا عُقُوقٌ.

الثّالِثُ: في مَحَبَّتِكَ القَدِيمَةِ، قالَهُ قَتادَةُ وسُفْيانُ.

الرّابِعُ: في شَقائِكَ القَدِيمِ، قالَهُ مُقاتِلٌ، ومِنهُ قَوْلُ لَبِيدٍ:

تَمَنّى أنْ تُلاقِيَ آلَ سَلْمى * بِحَطْمَةَ والمُنى طَرَفُ الضَّلالِ

وَفِي قائِلِ ذَلِكَ قَوْلانِ: أحَدُهُما: بَنُوهُ، ولَمْ يَقْصِدُوا بِذَلِكَ ذَمًّا فَيَأْثَمُوا.

والثّانِي: بَنُو بَنِيهِ وكانُوا صِغارًا.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 96–98:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then when the bearer of good tidings came﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: he was Shim'un (Simeon), as said by al-Dahhak.

The second: he was Yahudha (Judah).

He was called "the bearer of good tidings" (al-bashir) because he brought him good news.

﴿He cast it upon his face﴾, meaning he cast the shirt of Yusuf upon the face of Ya'qub.

﴿And he regained his sight﴾, i.e., he returned to seeing. On this there are two interpretations. The first: he could see again through the news of Yusuf. The second: he could see again after blindness.

﴿He said: Did I not tell you that I know from Allah what you do not know?﴾ On this there are three interpretations. The first: "I know from the truth of Yusuf's dream what you do not know."

(p-79) The second: "I know from the word of the Angel of Death that he has not taken the soul of Yusuf, which you do not know."

The third: "I know from the trials of the prophets with tribulations, the descent of relief, and the attainment of reward what you do not know."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They said: O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins﴾. They asked him this for two reasons. The first: they had inflicted upon him the pains of grief, from which the sin does not fall away except by honoring him.

The second: he was a prophet whose supplication is answered and whose request is granted. Ibn Wahb narrated from al-Layth ibn Sa'd that Ya'qub and the brothers of Yusuf stood for twenty years seeking repentance for what the brothers of Yusuf had done to Yusuf, and it was not accepted from them until Jibril met Ya'qub and taught him this supplication: "O hope of the believers, do not disappoint my hope; O aid of the believers, help me; O helper of the believers, assist me; O responder to the repentant, accept my repentance," and it was answered for them.

If it is said: forgiveness for them had already preceded by the saying of Yusuf earlier, ﴿No reproach upon you﴾ [the verse], so why did they ask their father to seek forgiveness for them? In answer to that there are three responses. The first: the wording of Yusuf was in the future tense, and it became a promise, not in the past tense so that it would be a report.

The second: what had preceded from Yusuf was forgiveness with regard to his own right, and then they asked their father to seek forgiveness for them with regard to his own self.

The third: they knew the prophethood of their father, so they were confident in his response, but they did not know the prophethood of their brother, so they were not confident in his response.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He said: I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord﴾. Regarding his delaying the seeking of forgiveness for them there are two interpretations. The first: he delayed it to avoid haste and as a promise for later, and for this reason 'Ata said: "Requests made to the young are easier than when made to the elders. Do you not see the saying of Yusuf: ﴿No reproach upon you this day﴾ and the saying of Ya'qub: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord﴾?" The second: he delayed it, waiting for the time of answer and anticipating the time of request.

On this there are three sayings. The first: "at the time of the night prayer," as said by 'Amr ibn Qays. The second: "until the pre-dawn," as said by Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar.

Anas ibn Malik narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "He delayed it for them until the pre-dawn, because the supplication at pre-dawn is answered."

The third: "until the night of Friday," as said by Ibn 'Abbas, and he narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ) in a marfu' report.

They asked him to seek forgiveness for them, although what was required for their sins was repentance from them rather than his seeking forgiveness for them, for three reasons. The first: for the blessing of his supplication and his seeking forgiveness.

The second: seeking his tenderness and his pleasure.

The third: out of their fear of trial and tribulation in this world.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 99–100:**

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his parents to himself﴾. Scholars differed about the gathering of Joseph with his parents and his family. Al-Kalbi and al-Suddi reported that Joseph left Egypt and the people of Egypt rode with him. It was also said that the great king went out with him and met Jacob. Al-Kalbi said: "It was a day's journey from Egypt, and the palace was at the forenoon (dahwah) from Egypt." When Jacob drew near, leaning on his son Judah as he walked, he looked at the horses and the people and said: "O Judah, is this Pharaoh?" He said: "No, this is your son Joseph." Jacob said: "Peace be upon you, O you who removes sorrows from me." Joseph replied: ﴿And he said, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security"﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

First: "In security from Pharaoh," said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

Second: "In security from famine and drought," said by al-Suddi.

Ibn Jurayj said: "Their gathering in Egypt took place after they entered upon him there, according to the apparent wording. On this view, the meaning of His saying ﴿Enter Egypt﴾ is: settle in Egypt."

Regarding His saying ﴿if God wills﴾ there are two views: First, that it refers to settling in Egypt, so its sense is: "Settle in Egypt, if God wills."

Second, that it refers back to Jacob's saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you, if God wills; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾, and the wording is then placed later (in sequence). This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

Ibn Mas'ud reported that they entered Egypt as ninety-three persons, men and women, and they left with Moses as six hundred and seventy thousand.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: Regarding "his parents" there are two views. First, that they were his father and his maternal aunt Rahil, since his father had married her after his mother, and so she was called "mother." His mother had died in childbirth with his brother Benjamin. This was said by Wahb and al-Suddi.

Second, that they were his father and his mother, and she was still alive until the entry into Egypt. This was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq.

﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: They prostrated to Joseph out of reverence for him. Qatadah said: "Prostration was a greeting for those before you, and God gave this community peace as the greeting of the people of Paradise."

Al-Hasan said: "Rather, God commanded them to prostrate to him in order to interpret the dream."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "His parents and his eleven brothers prostrated to him."

The second opinion: They prostrated to God, mighty and majestic. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Joseph was in the direction of the qiblah, so they faced him in prostration, and their prostration was thanks. The meaning of His saying ﴿and they fell down﴾ is "they fell," as He said: ﴿So the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾, meaning it collapsed.

The third opinion: Prostration here means submission and humbling oneself, and the meaning of His saying ﴿and they fell down﴾ is "they hastened."

﴿And he said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before; my Lord has made it true."﴾ Scholars differed about the period between his dream and its interpretation, in five opinions:

First: There were eighty years between them, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Second: There were forty years, said by Sulayman.

Third: Thirty-six years, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

(p-83) Fourth: Twenty-two years.

Fifth: There were eighteen years between them, said by Ibn Ishaq.

If it is said: "The dreams of the prophets are only true, so why did Jacob not trust in it and find consolation? And why did he say: ﴿O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they plot a plot against you﴾? And what harm can a plot do with the prior decree?" It is answered that there are two responses to this:

First: He saw it while he was a child, so it was permissible that it should differ from the dreams of the prophets who were sent (as messengers).

Second: He grieved over the long duration of the trial, and feared the plotting of the brothers in hastening harm.

﴿And He has been good to me, for He brought me out of prison and brought you from the desert﴾. If it is said: "Why did he limit the mention of what he was tested with to thanking God for bringing him out of prison, and not the well, when his state in the well was more perilous?" It is answered with three responses:

First: In prison, along with the fear of disgrace, there was something that was not in the well, so what was in his soul of his trial was greater, and therefore he singled it out for mention and thanks.

Second: He said that as thanks to God, mighty and majestic, for moving him from trial to blessing. He was moved to the king from prison, not from the well, so he was more specially singled out for mention and thanks, since by his coming out of prison he became a king, and by his coming out of the well he had been a slave.

Third: When he pardoned his brothers by saying ﴿No reproach upon you today﴾, he turned away from mentioning the well, because of what it contained of implicit rebuke. Some of the people of inner insight (ahl al-khawatir) interpreted his saying ﴿And He has been good to me, for He brought me out of prison﴾ to mean: out of the prison of displeasure into the open space of contentment.

Regarding his saying ﴿and brought you from the desert﴾ there are three opinions:

(p-84) First: They were in a desert in the land of Canaan, people of livestock and tents. This is the view of Qatadah.

Second: He had descended to Bada and built a mosque beneath its mountain, and from there they were sought out. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

Jamil said:

*You are the one who made Shaghab beloved to me, instead of Bada, and other lands than these two are my homelands.*

It is said "Bada yabdu" when one alights at Bada, and therefore he said "and brought you from the desert," even though they were city dwellers.

Third: Because they came into the desert, though they were city dwellers, and the preposition here means "in."

Those who held this view differed about the town in which they used to live, in three opinions:

First: They were from the people of Palestine, said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah.

Second: From the region of Harran in the land of al-Jazirah, and perhaps this is the view of al-Hasan.

Third: From al-Awlaj, from the direction of al-Sh'ib, related by Ibn Ishaq.

﴿After Satan had incited discord between me and my brothers﴾. Regarding his incitement (nazgh) there are two views: First, that it is the instilling of envy, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second, its meaning is to stir up and corrupt, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾. Qatadah said: "Subtle to Joseph by bringing him out of prison, and bringing his family from the desert, and removing from Joseph the incitement of Satan."

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 99–100:**

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿So when they entered upon Joseph, he drew his parents to himself﴾. Scholars differed about the gathering of Joseph with his parents and his family. Al-Kalbi and al-Suddi reported that Joseph left Egypt and the people of Egypt rode with him. It was also said that the great king went out with him and met Jacob. Al-Kalbi said: "It was a day's journey from Egypt, and the palace was at the forenoon (dahwah) from Egypt." When Jacob drew near, leaning on his son Judah as he walked, he looked at the horses and the people and said: "O Judah, is this Pharaoh?" He said: "No, this is your son Joseph." Jacob said: "Peace be upon you, O you who removes sorrows from me." Joseph replied: ﴿And he said, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security"﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

First: "In security from Pharaoh," said by Abu al-'Aliyah.

Second: "In security from famine and drought," said by al-Suddi.

Ibn Jurayj said: "Their gathering in Egypt took place after they entered upon him there, according to the apparent wording. On this view, the meaning of His saying ﴿Enter Egypt﴾ is: settle in Egypt."

Regarding His saying ﴿if God wills﴾ there are two views: First, that it refers to settling in Egypt, so its sense is: "Settle in Egypt, if God wills."

Second, that it refers back to Jacob's saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you, if God wills; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾, and the wording is then placed later (in sequence). This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

Ibn Mas'ud reported that they entered Egypt as ninety-three persons, men and women, and they left with Moses as six hundred and seventy thousand.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: Regarding "his parents" there are two views. First, that they were his father and his maternal aunt Rahil, since his father had married her after his mother, and so she was called "mother." His mother had died in childbirth with his brother Benjamin. This was said by Wahb and al-Suddi.

Second, that they were his father and his mother, and she was still alive until the entry into Egypt. This was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq.

﴿And they fell down before him in prostration﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: They prostrated to Joseph out of reverence for him. Qatadah said: "Prostration was a greeting for those before you, and God gave this community peace as the greeting of the people of Paradise."

Al-Hasan said: "Rather, God commanded them to prostrate to him in order to interpret the dream."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "His parents and his eleven brothers prostrated to him."

The second opinion: They prostrated to God, mighty and majestic. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Joseph was in the direction of the qiblah, so they faced him in prostration, and their prostration was thanks. The meaning of His saying ﴿and they fell down﴾ is "they fell," as He said: ﴿So the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾, meaning it collapsed.

The third opinion: Prostration here means submission and humbling oneself, and the meaning of His saying ﴿and they fell down﴾ is "they hastened."

﴿And he said, "O my father, this is the interpretation of my dream from before; my Lord has made it true."﴾ Scholars differed about the period between his dream and its interpretation, in five opinions:

First: There were eighty years between them, said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Second: There were forty years, said by Sulayman.

Third: Thirty-six years, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

(p-83) Fourth: Twenty-two years.

Fifth: There were eighteen years between them, said by Ibn Ishaq.

If it is said: "The dreams of the prophets are only true, so why did Jacob not trust in it and find consolation? And why did he say: ﴿O my son, do not relate your dream to your brothers, lest they plot a plot against you﴾? And what harm can a plot do with the prior decree?" It is answered that there are two responses to this:

First: He saw it while he was a child, so it was permissible that it should differ from the dreams of the prophets who were sent (as messengers).

Second: He grieved over the long duration of the trial, and feared the plotting of the brothers in hastening harm.

﴿And He has been good to me, for He brought me out of prison and brought you from the desert﴾. If it is said: "Why did he limit the mention of what he was tested with to thanking God for bringing him out of prison, and not the well, when his state in the well was more perilous?" It is answered with three responses:

First: In prison, along with the fear of disgrace, there was something that was not in the well, so what was in his soul of his trial was greater, and therefore he singled it out for mention and thanks.

Second: He said that as thanks to God, mighty and majestic, for moving him from trial to blessing. He was moved to the king from prison, not from the well, so he was more specially singled out for mention and thanks, since by his coming out of prison he became a king, and by his coming out of the well he had been a slave.

Third: When he pardoned his brothers by saying ﴿No reproach upon you today﴾, he turned away from mentioning the well, because of what it contained of implicit rebuke. Some of the people of inner insight (ahl al-khawatir) interpreted his saying ﴿And He has been good to me, for He brought me out of prison﴾ to mean: out of the prison of displeasure into the open space of contentment.

Regarding his saying ﴿and brought you from the desert﴾ there are three opinions:

(p-84) First: They were in a desert in the land of Canaan, people of livestock and tents. This is the view of Qatadah.

Second: He had descended to Bada and built a mosque beneath its mountain, and from there they were sought out. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

Jamil said:

*You are the one who made Shaghab beloved to me, instead of Bada, and other lands than these two are my homelands.*

It is said "Bada yabdu" when one alights at Bada, and therefore he said "and brought you from the desert," even though they were city dwellers.

Third: Because they came into the desert, though they were city dwellers, and the preposition here means "in."

Those who held this view differed about the town in which they used to live, in three opinions:

First: They were from the people of Palestine, said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah.

Second: From the region of Harran in the land of al-Jazirah, and perhaps this is the view of al-Hasan.

Third: From al-Awlaj, from the direction of al-Sh'ib, related by Ibn Ishaq.

﴿After Satan had incited discord between me and my brothers﴾. Regarding his incitement (nazgh) there are two views: First, that it is the instilling of envy, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second, its meaning is to stir up and corrupt, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾. Qatadah said: "Subtle to Joseph by bringing him out of prison, and bringing his family from the desert, and removing from Joseph the incitement of Satan."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 101:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿My Lord, You have indeed bestowed on me of the kingdom﴾ — concerning it there are four opinions:

(p-85) First: that "the kingdom" means the envy of his envious ones toward him. This was said by Ibn 'Ata'.

Second: he meant the confirmation of the dream that he had seen.

Third: that it is contentment with the decree and satisfaction with what is given.

Fourth: that he meant the kingdom of the land, and this is the most well-known.

He said "of the kingdom" only because he was over Egypt on behalf of Pharaoh.

﴿And You have taught me of the interpretation of events﴾ — concerning it there are two aspects: First: the interpretation of dreams. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: the reporting of the events of time (future occurrences). Related by Ibn 'Isa.

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ — that is, their Creator.

﴿You are my Protector in this world and the Hereafter﴾ — this may bear two meanings: First: my Master (mawlaya).

Second: my Helper.

﴿Cause me to die a Muslim﴾ — concerning it there are two aspects: First: meaning sincere in obedience. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Second: upon the religion of Islam.

Al-Hasan related that when the bearer of glad tidings came to Ya'qub, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said to him: "On what religion did you leave Yusuf?" He said: "On the religion of Islam."

He said: "Now the blessing is complete."

﴿And join me with the righteous﴾ — concerning it there are two sayings: First: with the people of Paradise. This was said by 'Ikrima.

Second: with his forefathers Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Qatada and al-Suddi said: "Yusuf was the first prophet to wish for death."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Ya'qub remained in the land of Egypt for seventeen years.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Ya'qub died in the land of Egypt, and he was carried to the land of Canaan and buried there.

Yusuf was buried in the land of Egypt, and he remained there until Musa extracted his bones, carried them, and buried them beside Ya'qub, peace be upon them both.

(p-87) ﴿That is among the tidings of the unseen﴾: meaning, this account which We have related to you, O Muhammad, concerning the matter of Yusuf, is among the reports of the unseen.

﴿We reveal it to you﴾: that is, We inform you through a revelation from Us to you.

﴿And you were not with them﴾: that is, with the brothers of Yusuf.

﴿When they agreed upon their affair﴾: concerning the casting of Yusuf into the well.

﴿While they were scheming﴾: this may have two meanings. One: (the scheming) against Yusuf, in casting him into the depths of the well. The second: (the scheming) against Ya'qub, when they came to him with his shirt stained with false blood.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verses 105–107:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And most of them do not believe in Allah except while they associate others with Him﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations.

The first: it is the saying of the polytheists: "Allah is our Lord, and our gods provide for us." This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: it refers to the hypocrites, who believe outwardly for the sake of show (riya'), while inwardly they disbelieve in Allah, may He be exalted. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: it is that one likens Allah, may He be exalted, to His creation. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fourth: it is that one associates others in obedience to Him, like the saying of a man: "Were it not for Allah and so-and-so, so-and-so would have perished." This is the view of Abu Ja'far.

The fifth: that they used to believe in Allah, may He be exalted, but disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ), so their belief is not valid. This is related by Ibn al-Anbari.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 108:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Say: This is my way﴾, has two interpretations:

(p-88) The first: "This is my call (da'wah)." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "This is my sunnah (way/practice)." This was said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

What is meant by it has two interpretations: The first: sincerity to Allah, may He be exalted, in monotheism (tawhid).

The second: submission to His command in what He has decreed.

﴿I call to Allah with insight, I and whoever follows me﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations: The first: "upon guidance," said by Qatadah.

The second: "upon truth," which is the saying of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

Some of the people of insight (ashab al-khawatir) mentioned a third interpretation: that is, I convey the message and I do not possess guidance.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 109:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed, from the people of the towns﴾. Qatadah said: "From the people of the cities, not the desert dwellers, because they are more knowledgeable and more forbearing."

Al-Hasan said: "Allah, Exalted is He, never sent a prophet from among the people of the desert, nor from among women, nor from among the jinn."

﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾. He means by "the abode" the Garden, and by "the Hereafter" the Resurrection. He called the Garden an "abode" even though the Fire is also an "abode," because the Garden is a homeland of choice, whereas the Fire is a dwelling of compulsion.

The second possibility: that He punishes their people, as said by Mujahid.

And a third possibility may be understood: that they despaired of victory.

﴿And they thought that they had been denied.﴾ Regarding "kudhibu" there are two readings. The first: with a dammah on the kaf, a kasrah on the dhal, and shaddah on it (kudhdhibu). This was recited by the two men of Mecca and Medina (al-Haramayn), Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir. Concerning its interpretation there are two views. The first: that is, their people thought that the messengers had lied to them (kadhdhabuhum). This is related from Ibn 'Isa.

The second reading is "kudhibu" with a dammah on the kaf and a light dhal (without shaddah). It was recited by the Kufans. Concerning its interpretation there are two views. The first: the followers of the messengers thought that they had been denied in what they had told them.

The second: the messengers thought that their followers had been denied in the faith in them that they had shown.

﴿Our victory came to them.﴾ Regarding this there are two views. The first: the victory of Allah, Exalted is He, came to the messengers, as said by Mujahid.

The second: the punishment of Allah, Exalted is He, came to their people, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿So whom We willed was delivered.⁠﴾ It is said: the prophets and those who believed with them.

﴿And Our might is not turned back from the people who are criminals.⁠﴾ That is, Our punishment when it descends upon them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 12, verse 111:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Indeed, in their stories there is a lesson for those of understanding.﴾ He means: in the stories of Yusuf and his brothers there is a lesson (i'tibar) for those endowed with intellect, that from the transfer of Yusuf from the well and the prison, and from humiliation and bondage, until He made him a king obeyed and a prophet sent forth, [it shows that] He is capable of granting victory to His messenger, exalting His religion, and destroying His enemies; and that delay is only a warning and an excuse.

﴿It was not a narration that could be invented⦆ — that it would be fabricated and conjectured. In this there are two views. The first: it means the Qur'an, as said by Qatadah.

The second: the stories that preceded, as said by Ibn Ishaq.

﴿But it is a confirmation of what was before it⦆ — in this there are two views. The first: that it confirms what came before it of the Torah, the Gospel, and the rest of God's books, the most high. This is the interpretation of those who held that it refers to the Qur'an.

The second: meaning, but what came before it of God's books confirms it. This is the view of those who held that it refers to the stories.

﴿And a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe⦆. And God knows best.

The Surah of Yusuf is completed, by the praise of God, His help, and the goodness of His success.
